speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The introduction into Canada of imitation cheese is now a real possibility and is being considered seriously by some companies, and since it could seriously threaten the income of industrial milk producers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That the government undertake comprehensive studies on the possibility of disastrous economic effects on the already hard hit industrial milk producers and the possible nutritional effects of imitation cheese on Canadians.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION THAT SPOUSE OF DECEASED PENSIONER RECEIVE TWO-THIRDS OF TOTAL PENSION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgency and importance.
In view of the great number of people between 60 and 65 who are facing serious problems of survival, particularly in the case of pensioners' widows, and considering that it has become urgent to apply a new policy in this field, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House implement as soon as possible the recommendation of the Federation de l'age d'or du Quebec, a copy of which has been sent to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), to the effect that a person of 60, who has the misfortune of losing her pensioner spouse, could draw two-thirds of their aggregate pensions, until she is 65, when she can draw her full old age pension.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, namely the operation of the benefit control system within the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In view of the fact that numerous allegations have been made that "non-cheaters" are being systematically cut off from unemployment insurance benefits-a serious charge at any time but even more so at a time when we are facing record high unemployment rates and dangerously low job vacancy rates-I move, seconded by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth):

That this House instructs the minister to initiate an investigation into the operation of the benefit control system of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and to report back to the House within three weeks the results of this investigation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, under one of the services provided by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, our interviewing officers indicate to individuals what job searches they should be conducting. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Acting Prime Minister):
subtopic: RECOGNITION OF FACT COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES SIMULTANEOUSLY OBSERVING COMMONWEALTH DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to rise on behalf of the government on this second Monday in March in recognition of the fact that today is Commonwealth Day. This year, for the first time, the 36 members of the Commonwealth around the world are observing Commonwealth Day simultaneously. This is, therefore, a day on which some 900 million people on five continents, who speak different languages, who have diverse cultures, who belong to different races, will take special note of their Commonwealth ties.
There are no superpowers in the Commonwealth; there is no primus inter pares-and that is one of its assets. Rather, it is an association of equal sovereign states which have voluntarily decided to come together and talk and work with each other in an atmosphere of mutual respect and understanding. In a world where negotiations among nations are too often a dia-

logue of the deaf, the Commonwealth provides a forum in which each member can express its views and be assured that its views will be heard. The Commonwealth promotes co-operation in place of discord, consultation in place of ignorance, and consensus in place of disharmony. Last year the Commonwealth was pleased to welcome a new member, the Seychelles which, like Canada and Mauritius, is a bilingual country and which, like Canada and Mauritius, is a full-fledged member of both the Commonwealth and "la francophonie".
We believe the Commonwealth provides an important avenue of attack on several world problems. Secretary General Ramphal recently pointed out:
The Commonwealth has one-fourth of the world's people, but it has nearly one-half of the world's poor.
Of the poorest of the poor, those with incomes of less than $200 per annum, nearly three of every four live within the Commonwealth. This suggest the immensity of the task before us and it suggests that now, more than ever before, we must use the Commonwealth to attack the problems of poverty, inequality and degradation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is very much looking forward to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in London, in June, and to a further strengthening of the close contacts with our Commonwealth partners tht we have enjoyed in the past. This year that meeting will follow closely the celebrations of the silver jubilee of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth who occupies the important role of head of the Commonwealth. In London we anticipate a strengthening of resolve to find ways of ensuring that each human being is able to live free from fear and want.
Mr. Speaker, this is Commonwealth Day; it is a day of education and a day on which I wish to underline the great value which Canada attaches to its Commonwealth association.

Mr. Speaker, in the presence of the auspicious company in our gallery, I join the Acting Prime Minister in this parliamentary observance of Commonwealth Day. It should not be lost on us that this year, for the first time, Commonwealth Day is being observed by 36 nations of the Commonwealth at the same time. That, at the very least, demonstrates how small our world has become, how much the actions of nations can affect other nations, and the truth that we can no longer turn our backs on the world when it suits us.
The statistics are astronomical: 900 million people, five continents; one-half of the world's population; three out of four of the poorest of the poor in the world live in the Commonwealth; the diversity of culture, language and race-all this is testimony to the sweeping potentiality of the Commonwealth as an instrument of understanding and for improving the human condition. For those reasons and others we should all view Canada's membership as membership in a precious association to be fostered and strengthened.
March 14, 1977

While all nations have their own national problems and priorities, only the blind among us would advocate that we should turn our backs on people for whom destitution, illiteracy and lack of economic opportunity are a way of life. If the Commonwealth were merely to expose those problems, it would do a useful service; but I believe history demonstrates that it has far greater potential.
The Commonwealth, moreover, can provide us with a window to the third world which we and others not of that world would otherwise lack. Mr. Speaker, it serves as an example to all in this country and outside that our differences need not always stand in the way of reasonable dialogue. Perhaps its greatest strength for the resolution of mankind's problems is the fact that despite diversity there is a voluntary agreement to meet and to talk. While the dialogue to some may be ongoing and perhaps endless, I suggest that the solution to all problems in this world begins with dialogue.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join the Acting Prime Minister and the spokesman of the Official Opposition in welcoming Commonwealth Day. The Commonwealth is quite an unusual and remarkable institution. It has no parallel in history. Many books have been written about it, and much said about it. You will be pleased to hear, Mr. Speaker, that I do not intend to make my remarks on the subject at all lengthy because we are profoundly aware of the Commonwealth and we in this country believe in it.
There are certain common institutions which unite us in the Commonwealth. There is the rule of law. With, I have to admit, an unfortunate exception, the rule of law does govern
Order Paper Questions
the peoples of the Commonwealth. We do in fact, although with differences, enjoy democratic institutions. We have genuine good will to each other based upon our common traditions. We are able to talk to each other despite the very great differences between our countries. However, all is not sweetness and light.
I am glad that the Acting Prime Minister read the message from Secretary-General Ramphal who pointed out that the Commonwealth has one-fourth of the world's people but it has nearly one-half of the world's poor. Of the poorest of the poor, those with incomes of less than $200 per annum, nearly three out of every four live within the Commonwealth. This means that if we wish to take the Commonwealth seriously and if we wish to show our sincerity, we must do something more than we have done as a developed country to help in the attack. I quote from the Acting Prime Minister's statement: "We must use the Commonwealth to attack the problems of poverty, inequality and degradation". If we do that seriously and meaningfully, we will have made the institution of the Commonwealth a boon not only to ourselves but to mankind.

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cullen that Bill C-24, respecting immigration to Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last when I called it four o'clock I was going through a two-point analysis as to my perception of immigration in this country. The fundamental base I had laid is that this country, and no country, really, has the legitimate cause to have an immigration policy that in any way is based on a racist policy. That, of course, should stand without argument. The two points I was particularly trying to put forward were that there is a myth in this land that Canada somehow has the potential to feed within its borders many more people than is really possible. The other point I had been trying to make and to document with statistics and fact is that Canada will much better serve the third world, not by importing people into this country but, rather by the export of science and technology. It is on that latter theme that I wish to continue. I quote from Scientific American of September, 1976, an article by Jennings:
Since 1967 the annual expenditure on rice research and related activities by CIAT, the Colombian government and the Colombian Rice Federation never exceeded $1 million. In Colombia alone and in one year alone, 1974, the added production resulting from the introduction of the new technology was valued at $230 million. That is a splendid return on any investment.
Our best hope is in teaching the poor nations to help themselves. I wish to quote from "The Development of Agriculture in Developing Countries", by W. David Hooper:
If the people of the poor countries are to be fed, the food will have to come from their soil, their resources and their farm economies. The surplus production of a few exporting countries can serve on occasion to buffer the impact of bad weather or other calamities, natural or man-made, but there should be no illusion that the world's food security can be ensured by abundant harvests from the fields of Kansas and Saskatchewan, Argentina and New South Wales.

The conscientious person should find relief in the fact that poorer nations, given the proper guidance and incentives, have been quick to adapt to more modern methods of agriculture. I again quote from David Hooper:
The significance of the "green revolution" derives not so much from its numerical impact on food output as from its demonstration of what is involved in the modernizing of traditional agricultures. The widespread, rapid adoption of high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice gave proof that peasant farmers were not slow or stubbornly resistant to change.
As further proof I offer the following quotation:
Within four years of the first widespread release of the seed of new high-yielding wheat varieties in South Asia those varieties occupied practically all the land suited to their cultivation. In response to yield differences of 200 to 300 per cent over traditional plant varieties, and with the important incentive of grain prices that made high-yield farming extremely profitable, the Asian peasant proved to be as innovative as any in the world.
Today, the world's agricultural land area is almost all in production. Any further increase in food supplies must come from improved technology. There are few new agricultural frontiers left to be conquered. To demonstrate this proposition I should like to read excerpts from a book by Lester R. Brown entitled "By Bread Alone".
From the beginning of agriculture until about 1950, most of the year to year increases in world food output came from expansion of the area under cultivation. Since 1950, however, the major increases-probably four-fifths of the current gains in output-are attributable to intensification of cultivation on existing land area.
Today, the increase in food output that can be produced with an additional ton of fertilizer or gallon of fuel is far higher in the developing countries than in the industrial countries. Since fertilizers are already used very heavily in the agriculturally advanced nations of Europe, in Japan and the United States, an additional pound of fertilizer applied in these nations may return no more than five additional pounds of grain. But in countries such as India, Indonesia or Brazil, another pound of fertilizer can yield at least ten additional pounds of grain. It is unfortunate and ironic that, when world fertilizer shortages emerged in 1973, the more advanced nations acted to restrict their fertilizer exports to the poor nations where the fertilizer could have produced much more food.
Further, Lester Brown points out:
The first domesticated cow probably yielded no more than 600 pounds of milk per year, barely enough to support a calf to the point at which it could forage for itself. In India, milk production remains at about that level today. By contrast, in 1973 the average milk cow in the United States yielded over 10,000 pounds of milk annually. The world record is held by a cow in the state of Washington, Skagvale Graceful Hattie, which recently produced more than 44,000 pounds of milk in a single year-55 quarts daily-thus outperforming its early ancestors by more than 70 to one.
Likewise, we should note:
The first domesticated hens did not lay more than about 15 eggs, or one clutch, per year. In 1973 the average American hen produced 228 eggs. For some time, U.S. hens held world egg-laying titles but a few years ago an industrious Japanese hen set a new record by laying 365 eggs in 365 days.
If we turn to the Scientific American of September, 1976, we find there an article entitled "The Amplification of Agricultural Production" in which Peter R. Jennings states:
The central element in the endeavour to improve yield is the breeding of new varieties of crop plants. A first imperative is the development of varieties which produce abundantly when grown in dense plantings and supplied with fertilizer, water and pesticides. The plants can also be given other desirable properties such as resistance to diseases and to insects, and tolerance of a wide range of climate, soil and other environmental factors. In principle, every heritable characteristic of the plant is subject to the will of the plant breeder.

Research into plant breeding has greatly increased the world's capacity to produce protein for human consumption, first by selecting and breeding for increased yield and, second, by selecting and breeding for varieties which contain a higher percentage of protein. To quote Mr. Jennings again:
For example, more than 30,000 kinds of rice have been collected. The multitude of existing varieties is of incalculable value today.
To further establish this point I should like to quote from a paper by Dixon Thompson called "The Preservation of Agricultural Land", published on April 20,1975:
If Canada is one of the four or five major food exporting countries-although we do import a lot of food, including meat, butter, fruit and vegetables-it is because we still have a relatively small population. Even if we are able to increase agricultural productivity, consuming more non-renewable resources in the process, we shall eventually lose the ability to produce a surplus for export, because of population growth.
What Mr. Thompson is pointing out here is simply this: as long as the "have" countries import large populations they are placed at a disadvantage to the extent that they are unable to export the technology which would secure the greatest advances in alleviating the critical food situation existing around the world. There is, then, a need to retain a relatively small but highly educated and motivated Canadian population. I quote from an interim report in connection with a National Research Council study on world food and nutrition published in 1975:
Annual increases of between 3 and 4 per cent in food consumption in developing countries depend upon parallel increases in their own production. Acreages are unlikely to increase more than 1 per cent per year-roughly the recent level-and may well increase less. The cost and other difficulties of bringing new land into production coupled with the geographic separation of most of the unfarmed arable land from the concentrations of population strongly inhibit opening new acreages.
Thus, the key to adequate feeding of future generations in the hunger prone areas of the world is very substantial farm yield increases-about 2.5 per cent per year, on the average, sustained over the coming decades. In some poor areas experiencing rapid population growth with few or no land reserves, yields may need to rise even to between 3 and 5 per cent per year. During the 1960s the over-all yield increase in the developing countries was 1.9 per cent and it was higher at the end of that period, but recent events suggest that this momentum will be hard to sustain. A strong research basis is indispensable to sustaining the required yield increases in developing countries.
Mr. Speaker, that statement simply confirms that those who believe Canada should have an open immigration policy because the world is hungry are people shrouded in myth. This is also the view of the Science Council of Canada. I quote the following from the council's report No. 25 entitled "Population, Technology and Resources", dated July, 1976:
Canada cannot through immigration policies contribute materially to the solution of problems created by exploding populations in other parts of the world. Such problems can be better treated through economic and technical assistance from the developed world than through large-scale migration.
Further weight to this contention is given by a report of the National Academy of Science which concluded, in 1975:
A model for such enterprise was provided by the work of the Rockefeller Foundation ... and also by the Ford Foundation in the development of high-yielding strains of cereal grains. Another is the research conducted by the population council in the improvement of birth control techniques and their adaptation to conditions in the underdeveloped countries, work initiated at a time when the United States government and public were not prepared to
Immigration Act
support such undertakings. These are outstanding examples of what we should do on a large scale in many other fields.
An overview of some of the agricultural success stories around the world should convince Canadians that our role is not to import the poor under a policy of open immigration but, rather, to assist the poor to accomplish the task of feeding themselves, and this we should do by exporting the research and technology which are so badly needed. Let me read a quotation from "Lives in Peril" put out by the Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Health Organization and UNICEF:
An important advance has been the introduction of high-yielding varieties of maize, rice and wheat. New varieties now becoming available signal the success of modern plant breeding. As a result of more easy and rapid genetic manipulation the essential characters of plants capable of standing the rigors of the climate have been combined with those of plants which give yields comparable to the ones achieved in advanced agricultural areas. High-yielding varieties have been instrumental in converting Mexico from an importer to an exporter of maize and wheat and they explain the dramatic change in the Philippines which now exports rice after having imported it for decades. In 1967-68 marked increases in cereal production occurred in some developing countries in all regions but they are most noteworthy in Brazil, maize; India, wheat, rice, maize sorghum; Iraq, wheat, rice, barley; Kenya, maize, wheat, sorghum; Pakistan, wheat, rice, sorghum; and Turkey, wheat.
Recent developments in poultry have been nothing short of revolutionary. While hens in most tropical countries still average about 30 to 40 small eggs per year rates of more than 200 medium-sized eggs have been achieved. Food requirements have also reduced to about two kilograms per dozen eggs, if efficient layers are properly cared for, from as much as one kilogram for one egg in primitive conditions. In India, for example, egg production doubled in the period 1961 to 1968 from five to ten eggs per head of population. The government aims to increase this further to 15 eggs per head of population by 1974 when some 84 million birds should be producing about 9,000 million eggs per year.
I concur wholeheartedly in the following sentiments contained in a report presented to the Joint Senate-House of Commons Committee on Immigration. It reads:
It is sometimes stated that because of its vast area Canada should have a number of times the present population. That is both stupid and impossible. Without any further immigration Canada's population is expected to double within 25 to 40 years. If that occurs, this country is not likely to retain food self-sufficiency and the present type and quality of diet without considerable increase in the percentage of disposable income required for food. Immigration will accentuate that trend and will have the effect of increasing the real relative cost of food here.
Those who want open immigration are short-term humanitarians. The more honest hope for a better world must rely on the dispersal of education, scientific knowledge and the desire to motivate others to help themselves. That is the principal reason North America has been an economic success in terms of agriculture and self-sufficiency in food.
Now I should like to quote from a report of a seminar held at the University of Guelph on February 28, 1974, entitled, "The Food Producing Potential of Canada's Land Resources". It reads:
In the United States, by 1955, the social return to the investment in hybrid corn research from 1910 to that date was at least 700 per cent. Since the main benefits from hybrid corn production have been reaped during the recent 20 years, the over-all dividend of the past 65 years investment in that research is clearly amongst the best returns obtained from any publicly supported endeavour.

March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
What we see then is that this country and other countries in the world have a tremendous obligation to export research, technology and education. However, a policy of open immigration is not one that we can adopt in this country and assume that in the long term it will be humanitarian. I should like to quote from the Science Council of Canada's report No. 25 entitled "Population, Technology and Resources", July, 1976:
As for immigration, neither end of the spectrum is credible. Neither a completely closed nor a wide-open door seems reasonable. In no way, of course, could Canada ever solve the world problem of overpopulation. Even if we maximized immigration and allowed our population to soar to 100 million people over the next 25 years we would have absorbed only one years's world population growth at current fertility rates.
Increased immigration will, however, threaten Canada's present ability to feed ourselves and restrict our potential for helping others to become self-sufficient. I should like to quote from a paper entitled "Implications of Continued Immigration on the Future of Canada":
Population in Canada is increasing faster than yields per acre. Therefore:
1.	Increasingly inferior land will be farmed.
2.	That will increase the relative cost of food.
3.	In addition, population increase keeps taking the higher quality land out of agricultural production. That, too, will increase relative food costs.
An increased rate of immigration ultimately means that Canada as a nation will be the loser. Moreover, the world at large will also be the loser because one of the nations that has the potential to assist the Third World will restrict its capabilities to help from a position of strength. I should now like to quote as follows from an anti-immigration submission presented to the Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Immigration:
In the United States the president's commission on population in the American future after exceedingly careful, wide-ranging discussion and research, concluded that for the United States, in terms of quality of life and living, there will be, on balance, more adverse effects than benefits from further increase in the population of that country. Ninety per cent of Canadians live with a population density as high or higher than the average population density of the United States. Without repugnant regulations to prevent it, the greatest increase in Canada's population will take place in the now heavily populated areas of this country, thereby making the American conclusion valid and applicable here.
I return to the fundamental question: Who will save the world when all nations are overpopulated? That is what we as members of parliament should address ourselves to on this very important question. The submission goes on to read:
It is generally acknowledged that the world is now overpopulated. More than half the world's people live in countries whose governments encourage or assist their citizens to limit their family size. It is recognized that overpopulation decreases the quality of life and living, usually entailing restrictive limitations and opportunities for individuals to develop their inherent potentials. It is also axiomatic that increase in population results in reduction of individual freedoms; it is impossible to have more people without more rules and regulations.
I should like to make reference to a paper entitled "Immigration Increases Food Costs" and read part of it as follows:
Canada does not have large areas of undeveloped land of good quality suitable for arable agriculture. Therefore, immigration will increasingly necessitate development of inferior land for arable agriculture. Moreover immigration will inevitably result in urban expansion because Canada's major cities are generally in areas where the quality of agricultural land is superior. Urban growth constantly encroaches on good agricultural land which is permanently removed from production.

To continue with this line of argument I should like to refer to the Science Council of Canada's report No. 25 entitled "Population, Technology and Resources" and quote from page 67 of that report of July, 1976:
The reasons that have led the council to recommend slow population growth include the following:
1.	Canada as a whole, and especially the industrial heartland of Ontario and Quebec, face quite severe difficulties in meeting their short-term energy requirements, especially oil and gas, and will probably have trouble meeting their energy needs for many years to come.
2.	The population around cities, especially around Toronto and Hamilton, is spreading on to the very small amount of good agricultural land and suitable climate that is available in Canada. Reversing this trend will require careful land use planning and rigid control of agricultural land, plus economic incentives for farmers to ensure that land is protected and is actually used for growing food.
3.	Metropolitan centres can, and should, absorb further population through in-building without extending their boundaries, in order to minimize the occupation of good agricultural land, transportation and other costs.
4.	Even with effective land use control, Canada will have to use food more carefully if it is to maintain its position as a major food exporter.
I would like to quote from the same source as follows:
Three-quarters of Canada's population is urban. But more significantly, 55 per cent of the population are metropolitan dwellers living in continuous built-up areas with populations of 100,000 and more. If the existing trends continue, almost all of our population increase over the next 40 years is expected to occur in these metropolitan areas.

speechtext:
I would like to thank hon. members for allowing me to extend my comments. The report continues:
Most experts believe that by the end of the century, 90 per cent of all Canadians will be living in urban areas and that metropolitan areas will grow rapidly at least until 1985. In the year 2001 over 32 per cent of our population is expected to be living in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver; these urban regions will have increased their combined population by at least three million.
Second-level cities with populations between 400,000 and one million (Calgary, Edmonton, Hamilton, Ottawa-Hull, Quebec and Winnipeg) are expected to grow proportionately more rapidly with several of them doubling in size within 30 years.
Much of our past immigration policy inflicted injustice and hardship on developing countries. I would like to quote from an anti-immigration submission presented to the joint committee on immigration:
Since any continued immigration will be highly selective, it will necessarily mean that we will be continuing to practice the brain drain with the selfish advantage of this country and at the expense of the countries of origin of the immigrants. Those immigrants accepted by Canada are predominantly among the most talented and valuable people in the countries of their origins; those countries are usually so desperately short of such highly qualified citizens that their loss through emigration hampers development in the countries which reared and educated them.
In conclusion, I would like to point out that this country is operating with a number of myths. One of the myths is that Canada is a large food-producing nation. In part that is true, but the real truth is that Canada is a net importer of food
March 14, 1977

rather than a net exporter, in dollar terms. The second myth is that Canada has a large amount of agricultural land. The more than five billion acres of land in this country contains only 12 million acres of class-one and class-two soil. Much of that is rapidly being taken away because most of our cities are situated right in the middle of Canada's agricultural heartland.
The third myth is that the Third World cannot make significant improvement to the world food supply. This might be true if this country and other developed nations are willing to export research and technology. The way to feed a world of eight billion people by the year 2010 is not through immigration but, rather, by the export of research and technology. If we are to be truly humanitarian, we must work with facts and not myths.
I wanted to make three points in my speech. First, we have no right to take a position which is in any way racist, bigoted or biased. That should not be the prerogative of any nation anywhere in the world. On the other hand, we must recognize that a policy of allowing large numbers of people into our country will decrease our capacity to produce and export food. More importantly, when we do an analysis of "have" nations, "have-not" nations and world production of food, we note that over the last two decades almost all of the world's increase in food production has come about not by an increase in the number of acres but by an increase in the export of science and technology. We must ask a simple and fundamental question: who is going to save the world if all the wealthy nations become overcrowded and no one is left to export the science and technology which is so desperately needed to increase food production in the Third World?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of all the ministerial portfolios, I consider the portfolio of manpower and immigration to be one of the most important. Immigration and manpower policies affect all of us, and therefore I consider it not only a duty but also a privilege to participate in this debate. Last Friday I met the minister just outside the parliamentary restaurant and advised him that I would be speaking today in this debate. He asked me to make sure that I said something nice about him and something good about the bill. I find it very easy to say something nice about the minister, but I find it rather difficult to say something good about the bill. I can say quite easily that the minister is a man of ability, integrity and compassion; there is no doubt about that.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
I would like to review some of the qualities of other ministers who have held this portfolio. There have been five ministers in the last ten years. Senator Marchand was the
Immigration Act
minister back in 1966 and 1967. He brought forward a policy of non-discrimination in immigration. That was a tremendous advance. He also brought forward the visitor concept. That was another step forward. The visitor concept ran into difficulties, not because of the principle but because of its application which resulted in many illegal immigrants.
I would like to refresh the memories of hon. members about Bryce Mackasey. During the 1972 election there was a serious problem with regard to Ugandan immigrants. To give Mr. Mackasey full credit, through him the government encouraged Ugandan immigrants to come to Canada. That took a great deal of courage and strength. Right after the election the same minister closed the door to visitors because of troubles with illegal visitors. After Mr. Mackasey came the present President of Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). He was saddled with the problem of illegal immigrants and with the problem of Chilean refugees. He met both those problems head on. He did an excellent job of solving some of the problems respecting illegal immigrants and he certainly gave fair treatment to Chilean refugees.
When I look at the present minister I think of the problems he has and his approaches to those problems. We now have a very high unemployment rate. There are well over 800,000 people in Canada who are unemployed and there is lack of government policy to solve this serious problem. The minister's proposed UIC amendments strike at the heart of working people and do very little to help them. That is the government's approach to the unemployment problem.
I cannot fault the minister for his approach to immigration because he comes from a city which probably does not feel the same impact as cities like Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver when it comes to immigration. I find that he has accepted a bill from his officials which I will call the bureaucrats' bill. I do not think it is the bill of the minister.
I thought the two main criticisms of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) last Friday indicated the main thrust of the criticism of the New Democratic Party. He said, first, that by the absence of regulations-which have not been published-it is difficult, if not impossible, to study this problem and give it proper treatment. The second point made by the hon. member for Greenwood was that some of the provisions had been described by others as restrictive and discriminatory, even though I do not think they fall within those classes, and that they have encroached to a considerable degree upon the civil liberties of most Canadians. If the minister will read the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood he will see detailed criticism with regard to some of the encroachments on the civil liberties of Canadians.
I said the minister is a man of ability, integrity and compassion. But it takes more, Mr. Speaker. It takes courage, foresight and determination, the other qualities on which I want to dwell concerning the minister's bill. One cannot fault clause 3 of the bill which sets forth the objectives of Canada's immigration policy. How can we object to a policy which stresses

Immigration Act
family reunification, non-discrimination, concern for refugees and the promotion of Canadian economic social and cultural goals? If you read subparagraphs (a) to (j) of clause 3 you would swear you were reading the new Mosaic code brought down by Moses with regard to new immigrants to Canada.
In his speech the minister set forth his approach to the level of numbers and the requirement, in consultation with the provinces. In my respectful view, in determining immigration policy they had to be based on two main items: first, economic and social conditions and, second-and just as important- attitudes. With regard to the level of numbers, it is necessary they be predicated on economic growth, employment policies, housing policies and social services. If they are not, we will have an increase in the tensions and problems which have surfaced recently in the main cities across the country. I refer to attitudes toward other races and nationalities.
I should like to compliment the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mr. Lee) on his speech of last Friday wherein he set forth a vivid and historical account of the treatment of the Chinese people in Canada. I hope all members of this House read the speech. I hope, too, that we are moving away from the times he related, back in 1885, and that we treat all races and nationalities on common ground at the present time. That is one of the main objectives set forth in the bill. As I listened to the hon. parliamentary secretary on Friday I could not help but think of the speaker who preceded him, the hon. member for Greenwood who is our party's critic on immigration matters. I could not help but think of the defence he put up for Japanese Canadians who were mistreated by the government back in 1944-45. If ever a person should be complimented, it is the hon. member for Greenwood for his contribution toward protecting the rights of those people who were mistreated by other Canadians. I think you would like to know, Mr. Speaker, that in the near future he will receive an honour from the Japanese people in Canada. As far as we are concerned, it is a well deserved honour.
When I speak about the problems of race and nationality, I must relate my experience in my own riding. In 1948, when I moved into the Broadview riding, it was 90 per cent Anglo-Saxon, with a small sprinkling of other nationalities. In 1977, it is only 40 per cent to 45 per cent Anglo-Saxon, with the balance made up of Greek and Macedonian as the second group, Chinese third, Italian fourth, and the balance a host of nationalities from different parts of the world.
It would be wrong to say we have not had our problems and difficulties in Broadview, but we have an attitude toward them and we accept the challenge. Last Saturday night I was an honoured guest at the Riverdale intercultural committee which held a multicultural spring festival at the Earl Grey senior public school. The committee is composed of representatives from different cultural associations in the riding and across the city, and at the festival the different cultures performed. Let me enumerate some of the groups that appeared: the native Indians commenced the program-and was it not proper that they should? Then we had the Koreans, Lithuanians, native Indians, Chinese, Pakistanis, Koreans again, East Indians,

Philippines, West Indians, and finished off with a great group called the Scottish. I could not help but feel that we were taking the right approach to the problems of race and nationality which confront us, and to fellowship and friendship, as a result of this cultural exchange. That is why I think it is so necessary to develop attitudes.
There is another group in our community, sponsored by LIP, called Harmony Canada. This is an Outreach project with the object of sensitizing the Riverdale community to Sikh culture. Dr. T. Singh visits different schools in the area to tell students about the different cultures. I think this is a valuable approach. May I say in passing that the churches in our area have been the springboard to meeting head-on the problem of race relations. I give full credit to reverend John Robson of Queen Street Presbyterian church for getting representatives of different groups together to find solutions to our problems.
I remember the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) making his maiden speech in this House in 1968. He quoted a great slave worker who had said something like this:
Judge not a man by the colour of his skin, nor the way he loves or fights or sins, nor by the gods he serves nor by the vintage he drinks, but judge a man by the way he thinks.
I think that type of philosophy is one for which we must have regard in race relations. If we are compassionate in our economic and social approaches, we shall have no difficulty in setting immigration levels for Canada.
A few minutes ago I heard the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone) speak about the intricate and sensitive problems of food production, about what would happen if too many people came to Canada, and how too many immigrants would create stresses within the economy. Mr. Speaker, the population of Canada, a country vast in extent, is some 23 million. We are rich in resources. The population of the United States is approximately 250 million people, or ten times our size. Yet Americans have been forerunners in technological development. They have met head-on the problems which a diversity of peoples and a large population create. It seems to me that if we take the proper approach, the threat of food shortages and racial disharmony will go away.
If the minister wants the new legislation to work successfully, I plead with him to institute a second amnesty program for illegal immigrants now in Canada. Our first amnesty or adjustment program was successful owing to the efforts of the President of Treasury Board. Why do I advocate a second amnesty program? Mr. Speaker, records indicate that there are in Canada between 400,000 and 500,000 illegal immigrants, and the expense of tracking them down is tremendous. For instance, in Toronto alone the RCMP detachment, under J. R. Nicholson, consists of 16 men. They, as well as many immigration officials, are engaged in tracking down illegal immigrants.
If we consider personnel in Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver and other large centres who are engaged in this activity it
March 14, 1977

should become obvious that the finding of illegal immigrants is a tremendously expensive undertaking. But the expense is not the real problem. Our illegal immigrants have to contend with a whole host of emotional, social and economic factors. I am sure the minister is aware of the article which appeared in the Toronto Star last December on the subject of illegal immigrants. I would quote part of the article written by Mr. Sydney Katz, an article which I commend to hon. members of the House and the minister. Mr. Katz wrote in part:
Every day last week, Victor Perez, 28, eagerly rifled through the newspapers and turned his radio on hourly to listen to the newscasts. He didn't want to miss even the smallest scrap of information about the new immigration bill introduced in the House of Commons by Minister of Immigration and Manpower, Bud Cullen.
Perez (not his real name) fervently prayed for revised immigration regulations that would mercifully end the hellish life that he and his wife, Isabella, had been leading for the past three years...
And how long can the illegals emotionally, socially and economically live with the uncertainty of always being only one knock on the door away from deportation?
Perez confesses that he's reached the end of his endurance. Because of the constant pressure, he suffers chronic fatigue. Isabella is plagued by "nervousness" and headaches. "To hell with it," he said recently. "I'm going to turn myself in and go home. We can't stand it any more".
We must deal with illegal immigrants on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. Mr. Katz talks of the damage being done to the children of illegal immigrants. His article went on to say this:
"It's a real tragedy," says Mendel Green, a Toronto lawyer who has handled many immigration cases. "Thousands of children are growing up without an education".
Instead of being in the classroom they accompany their mothers to their jobs-picking worms, or vegetables or fruit or doing housework. When this is impossible, the child may stay home alone all day.
Some suggest that illegal immigrants participate in criminal activities. I do not doubt that a small fraction do, but I am prepared to wager that 95 per cent of illegal immigrants are honest and hardworking people who left their countries to come to Canada for a better way of life for themselves and their children. Our approach to them must be humanitarian.
What would I do if I were minister of manpower and immigration? If I had any doubt about any second amnesty program I would ask the Standing Committee on Manpower and Immigration to meet with and call witnesses from the RCMP and the various organizations which deal with these people. They could testify quietly; perhaps their names should not be revealed. After all, we want the benefit of their opinions.
Clara Nickel, of the Bloor-Bathurst information centre, says some people become illegals quite unintentionally. She said, as reported in Mr. Katz' article:
I have seen articles in Portuguese newspapers which describe how easy it is to become a Canadian citizen. People believe it and end up in trouble over here.
The article went on to say:
Again efforts should be made to curb the activities of travel agents and phony immigration advisers who persuade foreign nationals-for purposes of private profit-
Immigration Act
I hope that the minister is persuaded, as I and the hon. member for Hamilton West, the Conservative spokesman, tried to point out, that the number one problem in the field of immigration is the illegal immigrant.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
I further suggest that the act will operate successfully only if applied with humanity and compassion. A second amnesty program would not only save money; it would save a repetition of old difficulties. The minister himself spoke of the new system of social insurance numbers which identifies persons who are not Canadian citizens of permanent residence and puts the onus on the employer to make sure that the person employed has a valid employment visa. I say that now we must exercise good judgment, common sense and humanity in dealing with the some 400,000 illegal immigrants in Canada. If the minister wants to make a valid contribution to Canada's immigration policy he must institute a second amnesty program. Such an approach would be farsighted and would go a long way to making this a better country in which all could live. Otherwise, this country will be saddled with the problem of illegal immigrants and the bill will be nothing but an exercise in bureaucracy.
I give the minister credit for correcting the inequities in the 1952 act dealing with prohibitions involving the mentally retarded, epileptics, and inmates of certain institutions. I recall a constituent of mine who came from Greece. He was on my doorstep week after week pleading with me to permit his son to come to Canada with his wife. They could not come because they had an epileptic child. After a great deal of effort I persuaded the present House leader that this family should come. I can still see the tears in that man's eyes when we got the news that the family was moving forward with the child. May I say that it operates on the family reunification principle. I thought it was great credit to the minister in permitting this youngster to come with his family. Therefore, this is a step in the right direction. We must, of course, realize that the success depends on the co-operation of the provincial and federal health departments. If the provincial departments find it imposes a very heavy financial burden, the minister of national health and welfare should give, and give generously, to meet the problem.
The hon. member for Greenwood set forth well last Friday our criticism concerning this provision; that is, the dependency on the decision of whether a person should come forward being completely dependent on a health officer. I hope we will be able to look at that question to see if we can expand that decision-making power so that we do not have any criticism as a result of this bill.
May I return to the main criticisms of the bill set forth by the critic of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Greenwood. He said in no uncertain terms that this bill lacks the regulations which will make the bill operative. The minister could have scored a real success if he had published them.

March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
We went through the question of regulation just a few months ago with regard to the borrowers and depositors protection act. We had the problem with regard to the criminal interest rates which exist. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) was given the opportunity to present the regulations with regard to these criminal rates, and he did not. They are having their difficulties in the committee, and they will have their difficulties when they come back. Before the bill is referred to the committee the minister should make available to all members the regulations relating to this bill. Otherwise, it will be impossible to deal with it in committee.
Need I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the selection criteria are based on regulations under the old act. I agree there has to be a certain flexibility to it. I recall the position that we had in 1972 with regard to visitors. By the use of order in council and regulations, that was stopped. I recall the employment problem we had. Again, by regulation, that was stopped. The least the minister can do is to set forth the criteria.
The main emphasis with regard to selection criteria in the past has been education. The special joint committee on immigration policy went into the problem in depth as it travelled across the country. They saw the unfairness of this approach. The best we have from the minister at this moment is that he appears to be pleased with the approach taken by the special committee on immigration with regard to taking the emphasis off education and putting it on work experience, and also with regard to sending people to designated areas.
The selection criteria are the heart and soul of the immigration policy. Therefore, it is necessary that we study them in detail so that we may have an excellent bill. There are two clauses I want to draw to the attention of the minister. They worried the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brown) and they give me double worry. Those clauses are contained on page 62 of the bill. Clause 115(n) reads:
-requiring any person or class of persons to report to an immigration officer before leaving Canada and prescribing the information to be provided and the manner in which such report shall be made to the immigration officer by any such person-
The explanatory note at the side reads:
S.	115(l)(n) may be used at some time in the future to provide for examination of outbound travellers if this step becomes necessary for the proper identification and control of illegal immigrants.
I hoped the minister would have dealt with this problem in his main speech, but he did not. It has raised fears in the minds of many of us with regard to the operation of these clauses. Is the minister talking about regulation with regard to visa permits? If he is, surely we should know the details concerning them. One can appreciate the wide power that would be given to immigration officials requiring any person or class of persons to report to an immigration officer and prescribing the essentials of information that must be given to him with regard to the report. I hope the minister will give us the full details with regard to this clause. Clause 115(o), which deals with the fingerprinting provision, reads:
The governor in council may make regulations [Mr. Gilbert. 1
(o) setting out the circumstances in which persons who seek admission or persons in Canada, other than Canadian citizens, may be required to be fingerprinted or photographed or otherwise identified-
This is so unusual to Canadian practice that it behooves all of us to study it in detail. I read with interest the minister's remarks with regard to this clause on fingerprinting. This is what he said:
Another less complex area, but about which some concern and misunderstanding have become evident, is the provision in the bill which can require persons other than Canadian citizens to be fingerprinted under certain circumstances. Many immigrant-receiving countries routinely require applicants for visas to be fingerprinted. We certainly do not intend to go that far.
Thank goodness! The minister continued:
Fingerprinting will be the exception rather than the rule, used only where there is doubt about a person's identity or his possible involvement in criminal activity. For persons in Canada we will fingerprint as a matter of routine only those who have been ordered removed from Canada. The two other situations in which we will require fingerprints are when a person is arrested under the Immigration Act, or when a visitor requests a change in or extension to his status, and in either case, the person is unable to satisfy the immigration officer of his identity. It will therefore be a rarity for a permanent resident to be fingerprinted. In all cases, when the fingerprints have served their immigration purpose, they will be disposed of under the normal file retirement program.
It is that last sentence with regard to fingerprints and photographs that really concerns me. The minister says they will be disposed of after they have been used by the immigration department. I would like to know from the minister whether these fingerprints and photographs will have been given to the RCMP or other police officials across the country. What happens with regard to those photographs and fingerprints concerning these people? It is all very well for the minister to say that when his department is finished with them, they will be disposed of. Can the minister tell us whether they will be destroyed by the RCMP, police officials or other judicial organizations across the country? This is a very crucial problem. This is why we would like the minister to make known the regulations concerning fingerprinting and photography. As the critic for the Conservative Party has said, this is another instance where the regulations have in the past not been clear. So it has been well said that this is legislation by regulation.
My time is running short, Mr. Speaker. My hon. friend from Greenwood has set forth the main concern of this party. May I, however, touch on a point with regard to prohibited classes and compliment the minister for clearing up difficulties in relation to the issue of moral turpitude as it concerns people with previous court convictions who have come to Canada. This area has always caused a great deal of worry to the people concerned and to counsel representing them.
One thing which does concern me is the clause having to do with terrorism, subversion and hijacking. The minister set forth his views in the speech he made. He referred to the reasons of security which removed such cases from the normal process of a full and fair hearing. I took part in the deliberations upon the temporary immigration security legislation which was passed a couple of years ago and which did not expire until the end of 1976. I appreciated the dilemma facing

the department at that time, as I do now. But the greatest test in a situation like this is, surely, the normal test, the test which has to be met day by day.
A few weeks ago a test was put before the minister by the professors at Queen's University. They intended to hold a symposium with regard to the critical situation in the third world, to assess the theories of development and their implications for public policy. They wanted to hear the views of Professor Andre Gunder Frank who holds opinions opposite to those normally held with regard to the treatment of third world countries, feeling they would then be able to see the total picture affecting these issues. I do not know Professor Frank's background, but it seems to me that if I were confronted with such a decision, if professors from a university contacted me asking that a person be allowed to express a diverging view with regard to policies concerning third world countries, I would have to be terribly persuaded that such a person should not be admitted before I would withhold permission.
In any event, the minister did not permit him to enter and he was prohibited from giving reasons for his refusal.
Is it any wonder, in these circumstances, that all of us have received a letter from Queen's University dated March 9, signed by various professors and setting forth their views with regard to the issue? This is what they say:
The case of Andre Gunder Frank is particularly significant in that it helps us to understand the workings of the new Immigration Act which is now before the Canadian House of Commons. The most striking aspect of the act is that it provides no procedures for review of the cases of persons refused entry to Canada on the grounds that they present a risk to national security. In the absence of provision for due process, the door opens wide to a series of possible abuses:
1.	There is no check on the accuracy of the information on which the decision is based.
2.	There is no check on bureaucracy's discretionary power. The act gives the bureaucracy and the executive the power to act unjustly.
3.	There is not even the possibility of an independent evaluation of the case by a neutral board judged competent to handle confidential material and acting outside of the political constraints imposed by the government in power.
4.	The applicants who are denied entry are given no reason for their exclusion nor the opportunity to clear their names.
All these abuses are compounded by the fact that the act permits the exclusion of applicants before they come into the country and thus they have no access to Canadian courts or any other form of due process.
I appreciate the minister's difficulty, but when I look at these facts, a department of sociology composed of professors at Queen's University inviting a person to speak on development policy, I would need to be, as I say, terribly persuaded that such a person was a national security risk before I would interfere with his visit. I am surprised the minister should have jumped so quickly to a conclusion with respect to this case. All this underlines the need to confer responsibility for these decisions to a committee composed of people who would be able to make an objective and impartial judgment.
In conclusion, may I say I find it difficult to support this bill because of the absence of regulations and the possibility of some infringement of civil liberties. As I said earlier, I hope the minister will bring these regulations before us. I hope, too,
Immigration Act
that he will announce a second amnesty program affecting illegal immigrants. I would then be able to say, without hesitation, that he is not only a man of integrity, ability and compassion, but also a man of courage, determination and conviction.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege and a pleasure to speak on this new immigration bill, Bill C-24, and to follow that fine gentleman, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert). I noted with interest one point he made, though I was a little puzzled by it. It was his reference to a second amnesty. It sounded like a good idea, and certainly it is a humanitarian idea-which is typical of the hon. member-but I cannot help wondering whether there would not be some undesirable motivation built into it, whether the word might not go around the world that it is a little too easy to come here illegally or, in other words, an invitation to hide out in Hamilton-

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext: -in Canada.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext: The truth came out.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Without prejudice. In other words, for visitors to hide out in Canada and wait for the next amnesty. Perhaps the hon. member for Broadview might want to comment on that point at some time. It demonstrates what is true in this whole area, namely, that immigration in the last few years has become a very difficult subject for a country like Canada, if not for the whole world. Probably it was a relatively easy area for us to take care of until the last few years, Canada being a young country, something of a pioneer backwater for most of the world. We have a very inhospitable climate and our ties were recognized to be essentially with the British and the French. We are a country to which few people decided to come while they were busy going to other areas which have now become less popular or more restrictive.
One of the very important events that changed this was something that happened in late March of last year, and it did not receive all that much attention. It was of momentous importance for the world, and certainly for Canada; that is the fact that the world population for the first time reached four billion people. For the first time there were four billion living human beings on this earth, and they were crowded into certain areas; they were not evenly distributed. Any one of us who has seen the charts of the increase in world population will realize how startling those figures are. Throughout most of the history of mankind the figures followed almost a level course, a plateau, with just a small rise-and only in our time, only in living memory, has that changed. That line has taken off, and at the present time it is skyrocketing straight upwards; a frightening prospect, one that is matched by other things in science-by, for example, the growth of a bacterial colony. When it reaches a certain point in skyrocketing upwards, it suddenly degenerates and dies.

March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
Some say this could be something worthwhile for us to think about; that could be a lesson to those of us who are alive today. Perhaps we are on a final course, although we hope that is not so. We are adding people to this earth at the rate of 70 million a year, which is three times the population of Canada, and by the end of this decade it is predicted that the population will reach from four billion to five billion within the lifetime of one childhood.
Canada, by contrast, as has been said this afternoon, is a big country with a small population of only 23 million people, with many people crowded in one area. It has almost four million square miles of territory-3.8 million to be exact-and a tremendous amount of opportunity. One would think, then- thinking very simplistically about this situation-that we might solve the problem simply by opening the immigration doors of Canada and letting the world flood in. That might make sense in some things like arithmetic. But there is a great deal more to it than that. On the other hand, there will be mounting pressure, which already exists for many reasons, for Canada to increase its immigration. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone) touched on that this afternoon, and I agree with him. I think he was on the right track. Certainly, Canada must have more immigration. Our immigration should be based on humanitarian reasons, such as letting in refugees, the reunification of families and so on. We must have people to fill the kind of jobs we will have in Canada in the future.
However, in spite of the fact that Canada is a big, open country, albeit with many parts that are unliveable, and there is mounting pressure to have people come here, the answer is not in immigration. The answer, by and large-even though our birth rate, ironically, is down to about zero-lies not in trying to solve the world's problems through immigration. This simply cannot be done, not even in the last country in the world with open spaces, namely, Canada. As the hon. member for Battle River said, the real answer-and I think we are all beginning to realize this for the first time-lies in technology, in applying science and technology to help those countries with the most trouble solve their problems in their own way. I concur with the hon. member heartily on that. Anyone who has travelled this world much, who has seen certain areas of Asia, Latin America and perhaps Africa, must be staggered by the population problems there. We know that if we open our door widely, it would not solve the problem. It would certainly make Canada unmanageable. Anyway, those people would not be able to come here, even with a massive immigration program. They simply could not afford to come here and I do not think we could mount such a program.
My family and I were staggered by what we saw during the seven years we were in India and Pakistan, as well as travelling in other parts of the world. The irony, when we got back and went into the birth control research field, was when we found that this country, with the least problems in the world, knew how to take care of its problems. We are well ahead in birth control and our population is not expanding very much. As a country with the least food problems in the world, we are probably the most able in food production.

The absolute reverse is true for countries most in need in this world, most in trouble. The birth control program, as successful as it has been here, has not been nearly as successful overseas. This is very frustrating. There is no time to go into the reasons-it is a wide subject. The same is true of food production. We can remember clearly the high hopes for the "green revolution" which was supposed to solve everything, but a few years later there was disillusionment. There was world drought, world shortage of fertilizer, and the "green revolution" was not successful. It depended on certain things to increase food production, in addition to the fact that many people in the most hungry parts of the world had the wrong understanding: they planted less instead of planting the same to provide more. These problems exist overseas-they do not exist for us so much-and yet we are going to face mounting pressure. It is a difficult decision for us at present, but I think it is one we can take with enlightenment, or enlightened self-interest as people say.
We are heading for a balanced policy and I think this bill will contribute to that end. We are trying to help the world with its problems and trying to maintain our way of life. We are trying to do the best we can with the immigration pressures which exist. There has been a great deal of change in Canada and in the world in the last few years, and therefore obviously we need new legislation.
This act goes back to 1952. A few changes were made in 1967 regarding selection. I think the most significant change that has been made in the time that some of us have been here in the last two or three years has been the one about not being able to apply to stay in Canada from within Canada. It is a very dramatic change. Probably we have all had a lot of experience with that, either with visitors or people with work permits applying to stay here, and we have had to refuse them. At first it can be a difficult thing to do, but I have found that by and large they have accepted it surprisingly well, and it looks as though it will be a workable part of our immigration policy.
There have been some worthwhile changes: for example, in the area of family reunification, which is an increasingly important humanitarian measure in which to try to bring families together. There is the matter of inadmissible classes, which has been touched on recently; the business of keeping out people with medical problems such as epilepsy, mental illness, the mentally retarded, socio-medical problems, moral turpitude, as the hon. member for Broadview said, homosexuality, and so on. In the last few years our ideas on this score have become more updated, more modern and more tolerant than they used to be. The matter of refugee status has been important in recent years as a result of civil wars, and so on. I think Canadians can hold their heads pretty high with regard to these things.
This bill did not just come out of the blue. It has been very well researched. In 1974 a green paper presented the basic ideas behind this bill. Then the joint committee travelled
March 14, 1977

across the country and heard Canadians in all parts, and now we have a fairly reasonable bill. I think the principles behind the bill have been generally accepted. It might reasonably have been expected in a country like Canada, which has many immigrants to start with, that there would be great apprehension and many objections voiced by many new Canadians that the bill closes the door, or that family members from overseas might not be allowed into Canada; but I have not noticed many objections along these lines from Italian, Portuguese or German people in my constituency. These people have been extremely intelligent and co-operative.
What does the bill offer? There are about ten major innovations. Although I will not touch on all of them, I would like to touch on a few. The bill offers explicit objectives which should provide some clear direction, some orientation and some philosophy as to what our immigration policy is all about. Simplifying the wording of the bill makes it easier to interpret. We can read it and understand the basis of all the provisions and details of the bill. We have a much better set of objectives, as limited as objectives can be.
Second, we must have a set of targets and ceilings. This is the kind of thing which in a country like Canada, with an immigration tradition, might bring about mixed feelings and some apprehension. These targets and ceilings begin to suggest the old word "quota" which is not held in very high favour in this country and never has been. Quotas suggest discrimination or favouritism of one kind of another. But of course that is not the idea. There will probably be some limitations as to the amount of immigration there will be during a given year, but the type of immigration will essentially be unchanged, except that it might be somewhat improved.
These limitations will apply to regular immigration movements affecting independent immigrants who come here searching for jobs which need to be filled, and they will apply to refugees. No matter what the world situation becomes, there obviously has to be some limit. But the most important thing is that there will be no limit with regard to bringing members of families into Canada. That is something upon which none of us can imagine Canada compromising.
What is the effect of these limits? As has been said, the bill will benefit both Canada and people coming to Canada as immigrants. The bill will help new people when they come here. It will help them cope with Canadian life. It will help them integrate smoothly without a great deal of effort and agony. It will also help Canada which has only so much economic and social ability to absorb many people in such a short period of time as a year. Third, this bill would bring about a system which would make immigration movement as objective and as fair as possible. It seems to me a very intelligent move to put less emphasis on education, on winning one's way into Canada and on writing an examination based on education. As Canada changes, it needs certain types of workers in certain locations. This bill will help people who are disadvantaged because of lack of education. Many parts of the world are not able to provide education to the extent that Canada is able to provide it. When people come to Canada, if
Immigration Act
they are not ruled out because of lack of education they will need to get along when they are here. Finding jobs is the most important thing, and if they can find employment in a certain area, so much the better.
The bill helps solve our demographic problems in terms of the distribution of people. The bill will help in developing the economies of certain local and rural areas, especially unpopulated or underpopulated areas, and with some luck there will be some relief of urban congestion. Urban congestion is a terrible trend which is afflicting Canada, like lemmings. Many are leaving rural areas and farms and going to cities where social and economic problems are piling up.
Fourth, this bill brings about a new commitment with regard to refugees. It is not just a commitment in spirit; the bill sets out exactly what we are going to do. I, for one, asked for that and I am pleased that the minister included that in the bill. The bill recognizes Canada's historical commitment to the universal declaration of human rights and the Helsinki accord; and, as the hon. member for Broadview mentioned, the business of ensuring Canada's freedom from the invasion of political terrorists and criminals who come here on mild and trumped-up pretences.
Fifth, federal-provincial relations is a very important matter. We are talking about that in many ways these days. We talk about federal-provincial conferences, decentralization and rationalization of responsibility. Hopefully, this bill will make a great deal of sense in terms of immigration. The bill will give the provinces much more say on the matter of their demography, on the matter of how many people there should be, where these people should come from and where they should be located. The bill is designed to deal adequately with the needs and opportunities of the provinces.
I will mention only one possible concern I have about federal-provincial relations, and that is the matter of provincial rights in immigration. Hopefully, this will be worked out in time; but what the current Quebec situation might do to Canada's reputation for fairness, openness and freedom is something which causes me concern. The current Quebec situation might cause feelings of conflict between the federal government and the provinces. For example, if a Quebec government should decide-and this could apply to any province; I just use Quebec as a current example-it would permit only truly Francophone immigrants, and if the federal government decided to challenge that, oppose it or even enforce its will, partly because of the reaction of other provinces, we might get a more serious situation than we have now. I look at this particular provision with some apprehension.
Finally, I would like to talk about some of the changes in the classes of immigrants. First, I would like to talk about the sponsored category and the reunification of immediate families. This is something which has had to be developed and refined in recent years because we have got into trouble over it. I will deal with that matter in a moment. Obviously, it makes good sense not to restrict the immigration of parents on the basis of age. It used to be that if someone who was a Canadian citizen or a landed immigrant wanted to bring their parents to
