March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
this country, the parents had to be age 65 or over. We have had experience that this has not always worked. People have come to our riding offices who had younger parents or brothers and sisters overseas who needed support, but they could not bring them here. This has been a terrible human problem which did not make any sense. It concerns parents mainly, but I have heard of people who wanted to bring their grandparents, and I suppose some grandparents would be young enough. Now, parents of any age can come. That is a step forward. It will be a relief to some new Canadians from all parts of the world.
I understand that the nominated category which was halfway between family and the regular type category will be eliminated. I consider that a good move. There will not now be a nominated category, but points will be given to people with close relatives in Canada. That is going to require some definition, too, but at least we are getting away from this business of family. How do you define "immediate family"? It is pretty obvious there can be no agreement whatsoever on the term "family", on terms like "parents", "brothers" or "cousins".
In countries like India and Pakistan, where I was privileged to spend many years, the feeling of universality and the religious feeling that these people have makes all of their countrymen their brothers. The line between the spiritual brother and blood brother or parent becomes very blurred. When they say, "So-and-so is my brother", they really mean it. It is very difficult to sort this out. When they come to Canada and say, "I should be allowed to bring in so-and-so because he is my parent", or, "my brother", that can be difficult, and in the past it has been. Hopefully, we can now define "immediate family", and there is merit in making some allowance for other relatives.
This will prevent the type of situation I was involved in in 1966 when I had to write to a constituent, Mr. James W. K. Cheung of Hornby, Ontario, concerning the immigration of his mother, Chow Mui Kwei. I wrote as follows:
-it was determined that she is unable to comply with the selection criteria applicable to nominated relatives ...
The immigration regulations provide for the sponsorship by a Canadian citizen or resident of his parents when they reach the age of sixty. Sponsored dependants are not obliged to comply with selection criteria and need only meet medical and background requirements. Your mother will be sixty in 1982 and, unfortunately, the only suggestion I can make is that you reapply for her at that time.
If there ever was a degrading type of letter that a member of parliament had to write, that is it. In effect, I told him to come back in 1982, not to bother us until then, and in the meantime to try to take care of his mother on the other side of the world. It is almost ridiculous.
In that connection, the relationship between this bill and Bill C-35 is an interesting piece of timing. Bill C-35 concerns the reciprocity of old age security benefits between this country and other countries. Most members have had communications from old people from overseas who want us to get the govern-
[Mr. Philbrook.J
ment to arrange this reciprocity so that when they come to Canada in their old age they may bring their benefits with them; but, even more, that those benefits may increase with inflation, with indexing, and so on, so that they do not lose out. It sounds like a very good idea, and once the bill is passed there will be this kind of arrangement for old people from other countries who come here, and for our own old people who go overseas. They will have these arrangements pretty quickly with the United States, Great Britain, Italy and France. Hopefully, we will soon be able to make arrangements with countries such as Germany, Greece, Portugal and others whose old people are already here. There are many advantages to this.
As someone pointed out, when the new immigration bill is passed, parents will be able to come to this country at any age. We will see parents coming here when they are in their fifties. Obviously, they will have trouble getting jobs-so what happens then? It is all right for us to work this out ahead of time and have the children agree to support them. But situations change, Mr. Speaker, and I think we can anticipate some pretty awkward and difficult situations if the older parents are here for a while and cannot get work, and then something happens in the family situation and their children do not feel they can support them any longer. I put this question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in committee, and he assured me that this possibility would be underlined before people ever came to Canada: they will be doubly and triply warned that they may encounter problems and that they must go through with their original plan to look after each other. I can still anticipate problems, however.
When the minister responsible for multiculturalism was in my riding last year speaking to the Famee Furlane club, an Italian club in Oakville, he told a little story. Many years ago, when this country first started, a British parliamentarian who was visiting said, "You have British people here now; you have Americans here now, and you want to bring Italian people and perhaps some others. What nationality will you be?" The man he was talking to, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, replied, "The nationality of this country will be freedom." I think that was a great, intuitive stroke of genius on the part of Laurier and it certainly reflects what is going on in this country today.
I, for one, fully support the multiculturalism program. It gives us the best of all worlds in an exchange of ideas and helps us develop tolerance and understanding. It is a very enriching experience, and I cannot think of any other country I would want to live in, for that reason. With the hospitality and warmth the ethnic groups bring, the Mardi Gras, Oktoberfest, Scottish dancing, life in Canada lacks very little. It leads in large measure to a more open immigration policy.
There is no question that immigration is decreasing these days, but it is a uniform drop, not a discriminatory one, in line with Canadian feeling. It involves all kinds of people in all areas of the world. To some extent, admittedly, it involves our economic picture and our links with the labour situation. To

Mr. Speaker, last November 1 when we were discussing this matter I was the last speaker. We had been discussing the possibility of having television in the House of Commons. Since that time the decision has been taken that we are to have television in the House of Commons. The House has set up a committee to consider the installation of television facilities and establish regulations and conditions under which pictures of this House are to be broadcast to the community. That part of the motion presented by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) has been dealt with.
Although I am a member of the special committee considering television in the House and the way in which our proceedings are to be televised, I confess that I now harbour some reservations which I did not harbour when the original decision to televise was taken. That reservation, purely and simply,

1 am thankful that the House leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition took the initiative to propose an amendment to the government's motion, for his amendment would encourage the special committee to propose ideas and to propose experiments so that we may discover the best approach to this question. I proposed, as the result of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), that an initiative be taken to televise one of the more important events this spring on our parliamentary calendar. subtopic: SUGGESTED MODIFICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: SUGGESTED MODIFICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall the mess the House got into last time because the antiquated procedures we followed led to details of the budget being broadcast on television even before members of the House of Commons knew what was in the budget document. I think it would be useful if the Canadian people were to get the news at the same time as the House of Commons. It would be appropriate to invite the television cameras in so that the people in the communities could watch and listen to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the replies of members of the opposition parties.
It would be appropriate, as well, if the Minister of Finance were to have 30 minutes only to present the hard facts of the budget, and if the leaders of the opposition parties or their financial critics were also to be allowed 30 minutes to present their reasoned criticisms. That would be a much more sensible and logical approach, preferable to the kind of helter-skelter activity taking place in the lobbies and outside the House when the budget speech is actually being delivered.
There would be no difficulty in dealing with the mechanics of the proposal, for at least the first hour of the budget presentation of the Minister of Finance is taken up with summing up the material contained in the budget papers which used to be published at least one week or so before the budget proper was brought down. If that material could be presented to the House one week or so in advance of the budget, the Minister of Finance would not have to spend so much of his time, of course, reviewing something already presented to us. He could spend his half-hour dealing with the realities and content of the budget and could give perhaps a much more detailed explanation of measures he intends to take. Therefore, I think we should take advantage of the initiative of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition and consent to
[Mr. Reid.)
the proposal to televise the forthcoming budget speech of the Minister of Finance.
Having said that, I direct attention to some of the other proposals of the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants. Frustrated, like the rest of us, by the way this place carries on its business, the hon. member wrote down five or six suggestions for improving the procedures of the House. I share his frustration with regard to the way in which we carry on our business. It is absolutely disgraceful that in the year 1977 we are carrying on, basically, as Sir John A. Macdonald carried on in 1867 in the first parliament of Canada. Basically we have made few changes; yet the world outside has changed substantially. What are we doing? We are doing exactly as those earlier parliamentarians would have done.
We have not considered the kind of society in which we live. It is a fast-moving society which takes for granted that something is done when an announcement is made. Because of our cumbersome procedures both in cabinet and in the House of Commons, action is often taken one year after the announcement. It is no wonder that members of the House, the House itself, our political system and our constitution are not taken as seriously as they ought to be. We are unable to deliver what we promise.
Much of the responsibility for the problems of the members of the House of Commons rests, it seems to me, squarely on the cabinet. It strikes me as completely unreasonable that the cabinet should take one year or more to reach a decision and, after presenting it to the House, expect the House to deal with it in a few weeks. That is an unreasonable assumption and an insult to all who sit there. Just because it has taken the cabinet so long to make a decision does not mean, necessarily, that it is the right decision or the only decision. The cabinet is often impatient with the House of Commons when it feels that cabinet decisions are being challenged. But is this not the place where such decisions ought to be challenged?
I suggest that one of the most important parliamentary reforms must be finding some way of changing our rules, changing them in a way which will be fair to cabinet, for it is the government of the country and ourselves, members of parliament, representing the people of the country. It strikes me that we can consider a number of things which make sense. First, we ought to have a calendar which makes sense. We must have a calendar which takes into account the amount of sitting time the government needs and the amount of legislation the government wishes to propose.
All of us have some idea of what is an appropriate legislative load for the House to carry and all of us, surely, have some understanding of the amount of time which we need in normal circumstances to process that legislative load. Nobody has any secrets from anybody else on that score. The matter is quite clear. However, the acceptance of that concept entails the cabinet's placing itself under the Standing Orders in a way which it does not now have to do. It means that all of us, as independent members, will be under the same kind of obligation. It means that we shall all be subjected to greater discipline in the planning and carrying out of that legislative
March 14, 1977

program. It means that we shall need to be given notice of legislation and even necessary background material to legislation it is proposed to debate in the House of Commons. The calendar, it seems to me, is an important item.
Second, once we accept the idea of the parliamentary calendar and the idea of the appropriate legislative load, it seems to me we must find some way to bring debate to an end. If we accept a limitation on the total time available to us and a limitation on the amount of legislation to be introduced, it seems to me that we should also accept some mechanism for assigning time available for the discussion of each of those legislative items. For the House of Commons this would mean giving a different priority to various items. At the moment we give priority to no item. At present an item is debated either until debate collapses or ends. Usually debate collapses. Really, we do not sharpen our knives, so to speak, and do not sharpen our minds. We go on debating ad nauseam.
For proof of my contention I invite hon. members to examine the reports of debates on any subject which has come before the House. You will find that debates which are limited are sharper and more effective than those in which there has been no time limit. As Samuel Johnson said, nothing sharpens a man's mind so much as the prospect of his being hanged tomorrow. I think the same sort of philosophy ought to apply to us. Items of great priority at present do not get the attention they deserve, whereas items of lower priority get more than they deserve. We do not distinguish between what is important and what is not. We are concerned only as to what we want to talk about at any given time.
I have often said that the most important reform we could make in the House of Commons is insisting that members talk to the subject under debate. But I am too much a realist, have been around here too long, to assume that that will ever come about. What we really require is to find some way for the House of Commons to set a time limit for the amount of time available to an item and then find some way to bring that knife-edge to bear.
There are a number of suggestions that have been proposed. One has been put forward by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants. In fact, it is his first suggestion, and I quote:
Cutting by one-half the time limits for speeches where such time limits are set forth in Standing Orders.
That would have an effect. Another proposal one should look at is one that was discussed in the procedure committee. That is that there be another mechanism to allow debate to go beyond the normal ten o'clock adjournment when there is a requirement for it. In many cases hon. members know that a debate is coming to an end and that all that is needed is another half-hour or hour to bring it to a conclusion. Why do we not do that? The Standing Orders now make it almost impossible to permit that to happen. We should look at that Standing Order with a view to loosening it up so that we can bring these matters to a conclusion when the time is there- and most members know when the time is there.
Changes in Standing Orders
One other suggestion that the subcommittee on procedure of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization has brought forth is a modified version of the British closure rule whereby it would be Mr. Speaker's responsibility to take the test of the House and determine when a question ought to be put. That might be too cumbersome for some. For others it might be too sharp. I say that the present situation is unsatisfactory. Perhaps we should look at it in that way. Surely under such circumstances there would have to be discussions with the House leaders of the other parties. However, I am certain that with proper good will it could be arranged.
Some hon. members have not had the opportunity to sit in on the discussions of the House leaders. Normally there is a discussion as to how much time is really required for a particular piece of legislation. There is discussion as to the number of speeches that have to be made from each party. Normally you come up with an informal discussion as to what is really required. However, I have never known any of those discussions to be fulfilled.
There is not sufficient discipline within the parties. None of us really willingly submits to the whips, House leaders or party leaders on these items. Consequently, the debates tend to take off with a life of their own. It is not the parties, party leaders or House leaders who are in control; it is the individual members. Once these debates get going it becomes impossible to bring them under control. What happens is they either peter out or the government is forced to bring in rule 75C if there has been sufficient agitation. This is hardly a parliamentary way to proceed to deal with the problems we ourselves create. Obviously, there has to be a greater amount of discipline imposed upon us, either by our collective decision through the Chair or through unilateral action by the government. Of the two, I prefer the first. Many members obviously prefer the second or prefer to have debate by exhaustion.
The last point I want to make is that we have not shown any collective will to come to grips with the problems of procedure that we face. We are still unable to decide just what it is we want this place to do. We are still unable to decide what it is the House of Commons should be attempting to accomplish. If you are looking for debate on the facts of the matter, you very seldom get it in the House of Commons. You very often get it in committee of the whole on finance bills and, particularly, in committees. If you want to know what people think about particular pieces of legislation, you get a pretty fair job on that at the second reading stage.
There has to be some attempt to draw these straws together and put them into a coherent whole. While the parties are constituted the way they are, they will be unable to do so; they will be unable to focus their attention on these things. At some point the frustration of members will get sufficiently great that we may make some unwise decision, some unconsidered decision, attempting to bring it into line with what we see as the reality out there. I am one of those who is frustrated. I feel the House of Commons is terribly inefficient. We do not discuss the important things. For example, at some point we ought to have had a debate on the question of the Anti-Inflation

March 14, 1977

Board-but we did not. We ought to have had a debate on the question of what is going on in Uganda. We have not had such a debate. As long as we proceed in using our time the way we do, talking the way we do without any particular focus, we will not get around to debating things that are important; we will continue to debate things that are in the past.
If you look at our legislation, the program before us, you will see that all of it has basically been announced before. All of it has been debated before in the press. One problem is that we have not been able to explore any kind of mechanism to bring these things before the House at the time announcements are made in a way that we can have a debate that is important. We get these things too late. It is our own fault. As soon as we decide we want to debate what is going on, we will make those changes.
In closing, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants for bringing this matter before us. I assure him that I share his frustration. I hope other members will share it also and will be moved to do something about it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I look upon the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) as an expression of difference of opinion that can be expressed. In fact, the way the hon. member has expressed himself and the way I intend to express myself is a clear illustration of what this House is. The hon. member would have a legislative grist mill. That is what he has in mind: someone plans, allocates time and brings the debate to an end, regardless of the wish of the members. However, somebody is getting the priority in the planning. The hon. member's thinking on this would be vastly improved if he sat for five years or so on the opposition. There is quite a difference of approach in the question of rules. The hon. member talked of frustration. Perhaps he should participate in the debates more than he does.
While I differ from my colleague for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) in some of the approaches he has taken, I think it is great to have this motion before us today even in its very shortened terms. I do not know why the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River does not really prod his House leader to bring forward motion No. 12 which is a referral of all the rules. I do not take as dark or despairing an attitude toward the rules and the way this House conducts its business. As I said, it is not a legislative grist mill. It is not an administrative body, but a deliberative body. Each member stands equally before Mr. Speaker with his colleagues.
To say you are automatically going to cut off everything is a denial of the right of people to be represented in parliament, the right that their member shall be their spokesman. I admit you cannot repeat the same ideas and arguments all the time. Surely, there are things that can be done to meet the total operation, make it more convenient and more to the taste of hon. members.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River should be the last to say that the operations of this House are something like those in the nineteenth century. After all, he is one of the
(Mr. Reid ]
acolytes of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) who when leader of the House was responsible for imposing the great portion of these rules; that is, the functioning rules of this House and the form of committee system that we have.
We are both members of the committee on procedure. He is the chairman of a subcommittee. I have chaired another, and the chief government whip has chaired a third. All three of us have been terribly frustrated by the fact that the caucuses on both sides seem to operate on the rule of the least common denominator-he who knows least about the rules but is prepared to yell the loudest carries most weight.
The reports of the subcommittees should have been proceeded with before now. Some of the recommendations were agreed to by both sides and there has been agreement from the caucuses to implement them. But there is a strange reluctance on the part of the government House leader to go forward even in this area, though to do so would cover a number of the points my hon. friend has raised; for example, with regard to expanding the adjournment debate and changing the hour from ten o'clock to six o'clock and utilizing the first portion of the dinner hour, putting on five speakers. Perhaps there would be about the same attendance, but there would at least, in my opinion, be better exposure and greater convenience for the Chair. Then we should have the possibility of carrying on our work after ten o'clock. I would say to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), "Talk to our counterparts in Britain and they will disabuse you within two minutes." They have a rule allowing for a 90-minute debate after ten o'clock. But there is not one of the members over there who has not complained, privately and publicly, about the hours during which the British parliament sits, sometimes until one o'clock or 1.30 in the morning.
There is no way this can continue. We have to consider our staff. They are human beings, too. They are not supposed to be turning out material like sausage meat out of a machine, or like sawdust out of a saw. They have to be as alert and as available as we are. And if you think you are going to have a member of parliament working until 1.30 in the morning and up on his feet ready to attend a committee meeting at 9.30 the next day, you have a surprise coming. Of course, no particular harm is done to those who do not come in anyway until noon, as some do.
For once the government whip was correct last year in contemplating changes in our committee structure. The committee system as it now stands is supported by some 80 or 90 members. When I say 90 I am being very generous; it is more like 80 members from all sides. You can exclude cabinet ministers and you can exclude some of the parliamentary secretaries. But for the rest the load is unevenly shared.
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to be a little more relevant than was the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. He spoke about a legislative philosophy which I think was not too relevant to the motion put forward by my hon. friend. Consider television in this House. There are some great things which have to happen
March 14, 1977

first. There is the law of libel which has to be amended before it comes in, even for the budget. There are other measures, too, which need to be taken. There may be one blessing, it is true. It will help to end the practice into which so many have fallen, of reading speeches which they have either prepared, or not prepared, themselves.
There is nothing quite so unforgiving as a camera focusing upon a person who is doing a bad job of reading. For myself, I very rarely read even a quotation. My grammar is not polished and my sentences may often be disjointed. On the other hand, it is debate, and if hon. members would consider this place as being a chamber for debate, not a chamber for reading set speeches, we should all be better off. When a series of set speeches are made there is no meeting of minds on any particular subject. If I had come here this afternoon with a speech, I would have to scrap it entirely because I want to debate with the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River some of the things he had to say. That is what we should be doing. That is how we should be conducting our discussions.
I disagree entirely, though, with the idea that there should be a calendar or legislative timetable. It is all very well for government members to sit over there as if they have been inspired from on high and as if the administration had a corner on brains and a divine right to have all its legislation accepted. Television will not cure this. It is a question of communicating to the people of this country what is being said. I could give example after example when, as a result of determined debate by a number of people who did not share the views of the government with regard to a bill, it finally got out among the people and the people learned of what was happening and said, "The opposition is right, and the government is wrong".
How many times has my hon. friend from Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) stopped the government cold because he and others organized a debate? Take Bill C-83. Was it not on the basis of those speeches that the government finally agreed that the bill must have been wrong? If we accept this timetable, this legislative sausage machine which so many government members advocate, this chamber will become merely redundant. It is a question of a minister making an explanation: nobody on the government side speaks, because to do so would be to delay the bill-a speech or two from the opposition, and then the vote. Legislation would go through on a steamroller. That is not parliament. That is not the democratic form of government. Canada is a big country with regional differences, and if we have some problems now with regional differences I can assure you they will be multiplied many times over if we ever get this legislative steamroller that some people advocate.
I do not dispute that there should be a rule of closure. What we were considering in the Committee last year was an eminently fair type of closure under which Mr. Speaker would have responsibility. I believe-and I myself have occupied that Chair-that there is a place for Mr. Speaker beside that of being a mere timekeeper. He has the sense of the House.
Changes in Standing Orders
After a certain time, a member-this could be the chief whip or the parliamentary secretary-might wish to propose a motion for closure. He would have to sound out Mr. Speaker to ascertain whether he would accept it. If Mr. Speaker felt there were at least six members who had a real desire to speak, he would simply say, "No; only after the six have spoken will I accept the motion." The motion could then be put, but there would have to be more than just a bare majority; there would have to be, say, 100 members voting for the motion so that there could be full representation. This is a Draconian procedure, but I think the placing of it can be done; however, not at the instance of a minister of the Crown rising in his place, as is done now, and announcing that the debate shall be terminated after eight hours. The present rule 75(c) is totally wrong.
We can move the adjournment debate. We can also change the question period. I have some feelings about the question period. I believe we have totally deformed the idea. But if that is the way it is going to go, fine. Perhaps I am one of the awkward squad when it comes to that. There are many other things we could talk about within the amendment of our rules. We could have a totally new committee structure. I think our report stage on bills is one of our most awkward procedures.
I will conclude my remarks by saying that I welcome this opportunity to speak on this motion, and I make a plea to the government House leader to please bring forward motion No. 12 under the heading "Government Business." I think we can agree to a reasonable debate on it, and then let us get on with the job, instead of everybody complaining that the procedures of this House are archaic. Every member has the right to his own views on the rules. I cannot say that anyone should have preference over any other, but there is one thing that we must have, that is, when the task has been given to a group of people who are interested and knowledgeable, if they have general agreement then let us not have the least common denominator in the House act as a veto on the implementation of the recommendations for rule changes, even on an experimental basis. We could have been doing a lot of good work trying out some of these rules in private members' hour, as the chief government whip has proposed, or in the structure of committees as I have proposed, and in some better use of time as others in the committee have proposed. But we have stood absolutely still. All the good work that has been done has been relegated to the waste basket. However, it can be resurrected. Therefore I will ask the government whip and the government supporters to put some pressure on their House leader to get motion No. 12 before us. We will deal with it and proceed to effect some of the changes which I am sure most hon. members want.

subtopic: SUGGESTED MODIFICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased indeed to have this opportunity during private members' hour this afternoon to participate in the debate on the motion put forward by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). First of all I wish to state that I agree entirely with what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) said when he spoke earlier. He is obviously one

Changes in Standing Orders
who has a great appreciation of the rules and procedures of the House and of their importance in ensuring that business moves smoothly through the House. I, also, am aware of the great importance of this subject, and this is why I am delighted to have the opportunity to participate in this debate.
The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants has made several recommendations in his motion, the first of which is to cut by one half the time limit for speeches as set forth in the standing orders. Obviously this is a very worthwhile recommendation, but one wonders whether members on all sides of the House could reach agreement on this. He recommended also the setting up of a committee composed of members of all parties and of members of the parliamentary press gallery to supervise information on proceedings which take place in the House. I believe that this is an area which should be tightened up. All too often in the past important announcements and statements affecting the House, which should have been made in the House, were unnecessarily delayed and in some instances were in the hands of the press prior to being announced in the House. I believe we should debate this subject and look closely at the procedure we are following so that members can retain their privileged position as representatives of the people who should be the first to hear official statements, and the first to see copies of official documents relating to this House.
I find it difficult, however, to agree with what the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said this afternoon on this motion. I was rather surprised to hear as experienced a member as the hon. member for Edmonton West who, as I understand it, is a former Speaker of the House and who has had many years of experience here, taking up the time of the House in private members' hour in such a negative way rather than coming forward with positive suggestions and recommendations, which I believe he might well have done, thus giving us the benefit of his experience. I believe that we should take the procedures of this House more seriously and more positively so as to ensure that they will be respected not only by all members of the House but by the community at large. Therefore, I was very disappointed that we did not have the benefit of some positive recommendations from the hon. member for Edmonton West when he spoke a few moments ago and had such an excellent opportunity to make them.
Another matter that should be explored, I believe, is greater discipline in the House. When motion No. 12 is brought before the House, considered, and eventually implemented, I hope that the matter of discipline will be debated, especially in view of what we have seen in recent months. One thing upon which there should be some deliberation and debate is the matter of discipline. Discipline is something which will be needed if the rules and regulations of parliamentary procedure are to work. If there is discipline the public will respect hon. members in their work here in the House. If we, as the representatives of the people, are to be true leaders of our communities and provinces in this House, we should have discipline, and that should show in our every word and deed. If that were the case there would be fewer difficulties and fewer delays, and the

respect of the public at large for the work we are trying to do here would grow.
I realize that this could be a topic for considerable discussion. I do not want to get off the topic of the rules of the House by belabouring the point about discipline, but if we could see the recommendations of the committee which to date has worked many hours, we could consider them, approve them, and perhaps adopt them, and we would then be able to enjoy the respect we all want.
On the matter of the so-called late show, the proceedings on the adjournment motion, I agree with the recommendation of the hon. member for Edmonton West that those proceedings should be held at a more reasonable time. Those proceedings are important, and rather than having a late show, perhaps the proceedings could be held from six o'clock to seven o'clock, or from one o'clock to two o'clock just prior to the question period. The committee should seriously consider this so that we might have a more reasonable time in which to give all hon. members an opportunity to express themselves and to participate in that particular order of the day.
The matter of closure was touched upon. No one likes closure. No one likes to see it used, but it is there for a very good reason. In past months it has proved its effectiveness, and I for one am convinced of its usefulness. It is obviously needed. If parties and members do not want to be reasonable and serious about a proposition which is put before them, and if they are hell bent, so to speak, on delaying the proceedings of the House, then it is proper for any government to invoke closure.
I join with the hon. member for Edmonton West, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, and all other hon. members who are sincerely interested in seeing a modern approach to the proceedings of this House taken as soon as possible, and I urge the earliest possible implementation of such an approach.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SUGGESTED MODIFICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the seconder of this motion I want to comment only briefly because we are getting close to the end of private members' hour. I want to commend the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) for bringing the motion forward. I commend also the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) whose contribution to the debate was exceptionally well put, well thought out, and added considerably to the ideas expressed in the motion.
The first suggestion of the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants is that the time for speeches be cut in half. I hope to lend some credence to that by sitting down after using half the time I might normally use before sitting down. Surely in a day of modern communications, of instant replays, and of 30 second ads there is a place for a brief speech by a member of parliament. Surely we can put before our colleagues in this House our thoughts on a particular piece of legislation briefly, even if we only say "I agree with Jones, I agree with Smith, I agree with Brown, and my addition to the debate is thus and
March 14, 1977

so," and sit down. That is probably the most important aspect of this motion. I have long felt that the 40 minute limit on speeches was too much.
Recently we were subjected to a speech lasting a couple of days, and I think that was to the detriment of the House. It was a very interesting ploy, it achieved a certain end, but I think there are other ways of achieving ends. I would like very much to see some rule changes in this regard.
There are three aspects of the hon. member's motion which I particularly want to support, and one has to do with the late show. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) commented on this, and in keeping with what I suggested I am going to say that I support what he said. Perhaps those proceedings could be held at six o'clock, and perhaps the time could be extended so that at least five hon. members could participate. Certainly there may not be very many hon. members present for the late show, but there are not very many hon. members here at ten o'clock anyway. That would not change. Those who are interested could sit in, and we would not want to take very much time away from the ministers or parliamentary secretaries who respond.
The hon. member recommended setting at five the number of hon. members who may oppose unanimous consent. It seems to me that to have 264 representatives from all of Canada halted in their desire to do something by one single member who may have an attack of dysentery or migraine headache is entirely unreasonable. Five is perhaps not unreasonable. This measure would certainly lend some credence to the word "unanimous". I do not think unanimous has to mean all but one. I think allowing five to oppose would not be entirely unreasonable.
So that we can have a serious look at this motion-and since there is quite a bit of time remaining before the end of private members' hour-I am going to resume my seat and will support the motion.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: SUGGESTED MODIFICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
M. Speaker, I too wish to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). He and I worked very hard on the sub-committee report on private members business. In that effort we had the counsel of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Fortin). We would have been happy to see more action taken as a result of some of the recommendations in that report.
I also want to congratulate the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) for his honest recognition of the desire of people like the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) to bring forward some good initiatives with regard to procedure and organization. I think the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has done this in his report which was brought forward in committee, but I feel it is a slight distortion to imply in any way that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was just talking about a sausage machine through which legislation would be processed. I think that it is rather unfair because that hon. member is honestly concerned with parlia-
Changes in Standing Orders
ment, with the right of members to speak, and with the fact that parliament should operate in a way that would allow all of us a fair say in what is occurring, and at the same time make up a schedule which all would adhere to and from which the public could expect performance. I think that is really what he was saying and he was not in any way implying that any government should have the kind of control which would merely order legislation through.
[DOT] (P50)
In fact I might say that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has quite often chastised people on this side of the House for attempting just to move legislation into a large barrel and push it through, rather than being certain that it is appropriate and that there is time enough to speak to it.
Another matter that concerns me is the reference to Motion No. 12 and that the government House leader should be bringing forward this motion. In his remarks the hon. member for Edmonton West said there should be a reasonable amount of debate. In the past when references were brought to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization it was agreed that we would not debate those motions; that the committee would come to agreement by having discussions and would bring forward a recommendation which had some chance of success, and at that time there would be an opportunity for all to debate the matter. But to debate before the matters come before us would seem to use unnecessary time. It is my understanding that it might be anywhere from three to four to five days.
I think the government House leader, being as responsible as anyone from Cape Breton is, would not want to interfere with normal legislation and stop to debate for three days whether we should send a certain reference to a committee to decide some matter of procedure. I think in all fairness we should remember that.
My concerns are somewhat different from those of other members. This may be because of my background in working with young people, in education, and possibly as a dean of students, and now as whip. I am terribly concerned about individual members. I think all people should have more concern about the members than their own special desire about how procedures should be organized in the House, or of their party and its special desires, or the government and its special desires. We should at this moment pay attention to what ordinary members of parliament-as all of us are regardless of where we sit, whether in the government, as ministers or as whips, basically we are all members of parliament-and we should be concerned about how each of us can best use our time here. We should have the opportunity to speak for our constituents.
It seems to me that if we cannot even come to an agreement, regardless of the initiatives which would help the government or give the opposition a better opportunity to look into estimates and things of that nature, all of which are terribly important-if we cannot even agree that there should be a way in private members' hour by which members can control that
3954

March 14, 1977
Changes in Standing Orders
hour, that it should not also be subject to the fact that possibly two House leaders might agree, or two whips, that something is going to happen-then it seems very wrong, Mr. Speaker, that government initiatives should have any control over private members' hour. There should be a moment in that private members' hour for private members. Yet we cannot agree on that because people want to tie that in with some agreement on what the government might want, or the opposition might want, or some other party might want.
I think we have to face up to time schedules. It seems to me that the press and the media should be made very aware of the fact that those of us who go home every Friday night do not go home for holidays but go home for work sessions, some of which are in the riding and some of which are in this parliament. Whips should be able to put on a card that members will be here from January 10 to January 24 in work session in parliament, and will be in their ridings from January 24 to February 2 at work sessions. We should be able to do that in a completely open way so that nobody says to a member in his riding, "Oh, you are on holiday from parliament." You certainly are not. You are visiting functions, you are meeting people, you are answering questions, you are acting somewhat as an ombudsman. We hear of countries like Sweden that have five ombudsmen. I maintain we have 264, or 318, or whatever the figure is going to be. Every member of parliament in this country acts as an ombudsman and requires time at home to do that.
One hon. member mentioned changing the hours, and particularly the time of the late show. But what about private members' hour? A lot of members who fly west or east like to try to get out on the first plane. If we sit until five o'clock they may just miss their plane by 20 minutes. If I go to Hamilton I either have to go at 5.15 or else go to Toronto and not get home until nine o'clock at night. If I leave at 5.15 I am in my riding at 6.10 and can attend a function that night, but because the House sits until five o'clock I cannot do that.
Maybe it would be better to have private members' hour from ten o'clock till 11 o'clock in the morning. That adjustment would have to be tied in with what we do in other procedures. That seems to be the hangup, that there is a negotiation. Maybe that is what the hon. member for Edmonton West was referring to when he spoke of the common denominator-if you get this then you have to get this; if you get that then you have to get that. No, I say. I say there is an opportunity for us to do something on procedure and we should be able to bring that motion forward without debate in this House and forward the reference to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. They should come back with recommendations that are fair for all members and do not have such great reliance on the success of the government or of the opposition. Something should be done for private members at this moment; then I think we would find that members, House leaders, and people in the committee could probably go further into the committee stage and the allocation of time. If we cannot even do something for individual members of parliament to make things more reasonable for them, then I do not

see how we can ever tackle the really heavy problems of procedure.
From what I can hear on any side of the House and from the people who have spoken, I think we do want to do something on procedure. This is a moment in parliament when people say it is something we should do. We are a product of the times; let parliament be for our times. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
Some hon. Mlembers: Hear, hear!

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Cullen that Bill C-24, respecting immigration to Canada, be read the second time referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset let me say that it is a privilege to speak briefly on Bill C-24, this most important bill on immigration. I was particularly pleased to hear the previous speaker, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook), terminate his comments by emphasizing the importance of family re-unification. I tell the hon. member, through you, Mr. Speaker, that I share his views.
Before being elected to this House in 1972, and even since that time, I have been aware of many instances showing that the present act does really not address itself to the important humanitarian matter of family re-unification. I suspect that my views about the importance of the family unit are shared by most members of the House, and those fortunate enough to experience the warmth and close ties of family will have no difficulty in appreciating the need for family re-unification measures.
Instead of attempting to consider all aspects of the immigration bill now being debated on second reading in a global context, I have decided that it would be useful to limit my comments to a few specific issues which have been raised, and

to some which have not been alluded to yet. One of the major complaints voiced by many speakers in this debate is that the bill does not contain most of the important provisions of the government's immigration policy. It is readily apparent that a good deal of the policy will be established by way of regulation and order in council. As the minister knows, I have objected to this method in the past and repeatedly emphasized the importance of knowing the regulations when we attempt to discuss in detail the merit of any particular piece of legislation. Having said that, I have no difficulty in recognizing that the government and the minister require flexibility in the administration of a piece of legislation. However, I find it inexcusable that the major, operative portion of legislation, which is embodied in regulations, is not available for members of the House of Commons to assess. The regulations should be available to hon. members if they are to understand the implications of the bill and the policies of the government.
I recall, both when I spoke on the Environmental Contaminants Act and on the bill relating to amendments to the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, that it was readily apparent to all hon. members that one could not discuss many aspects of the legislation before the House because of the absence of regulations. It should be noted that in many instances bills have been introduced in this House which contained clauses which did nothing more than enshrine in legislation previous regulations established without parliamentary debate. I suspect, unless the minister has a change of heart, that that may happen in this instance.
When the minister introduced this bill on March 10, he pointed out that clause 3 lays down in clear terms the basic objectives which the government considers should govern Canadian immigration policy now and in future. I think it is readily apparent that immigration objectives are useful in serving as a guideline for the interpretation of the act, but it must be emphasized that they are not enforceable by law. As the minister knows, future regulations may deviate substantially from the intent of the objectives as outlined in clause 3. I have no doubt that many of those objectives in the bill will be subject to examination during committee stage. I therefore anticipate that the minister will make available to us, and elaborate on, the innumerable regulations which it will be essential for us to know if we are to have a clear understanding of the government's immigration policy and the effect the bill will have on future immigration in Canada.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), in initiating the debate on behalf of our party, emphasized two important points. First, there is the necessity to develop a demographic policy which will ensure a future for all Canadians, a future in which not only economic opportunities exist but, equally, in which there is freedom, racial equality, and justice for everyone. Second, he correctly pointed out that the entire selection system by which immigrants come to Canada is not included in the bill. Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) clearly pointed out the importance of the selection system, the necessity for each of us to understand it in depth and consider it in depth during the committee stage.
Immigration Act
It is obvious to me that those two factors are interdependent; and if Canadians are to understand clearly the government's immigration policy, if Canadians in future are to understand the manner in which a person may qualify for entry into Canada, I say it is evident that such details must be made available now to members of parliament, and indeed to all Canadians.
I want to limit my comments to three of the immigration objectives we find in the bill, namely, that portion that indicates Canadian immigration policy is to maintain and protect the health, safety and good order of Canadian society. The second deals with the facilitation of visitors into Canada for the purpose of fostering trade and commerce, tourism, cultural and scientific activities, and international understanding. Finally, there is the objective of promoting co-operation between the government of Canada and other levels of government and non-governmental agencies in Canada.
This does not imply that I intend to discuss each of these sections in detail. Obviously, for those who have studied the bill and the implications of each of the objectives, this would be impractical in the time frame allotted to us. Nor do I want to imply that the particular immigration objectives that I have referred to are more important than the other declared objectives within the bill. However, as I indicated somewhat earlier,
I felt it would be useful to discuss briefly three important problems which I feel are supportive evidence of the difficulties members of parliament are experiencing in understanding the bill without having adequate information and without knowledge of the regulations.
I was pleased to learn that the bill abolishes a number of provisions which, frankly, are archaic and unjust. As the minister knows, and quite rightly indicated in his speech in the House of Commons, the 1952 act barred epileptics, the mentally retarded, and those who had been inmates of mental institutions.
I can also understand the minister's reasoning to include a portion of the inadmissible classes which includes persons suffering from any disease, disorder, disability or other health impediment as a result of the nature, severity or duration of which, in the opinion of a medical officer, they are or are likely to be a danger to public health or public safety, where their admission would cause or reasonably be expected to cause excessive demands on health or social services. If I interpret this correctly, a medical officer is given the ultimate right to determine whether an excessive demand on the health and social services exists. I suggest to the minister, in all sincerity, that I feel somewhat uneasy that a medical officer would be given unlimited discretionary powers to make such a decision.
Those involved in the delivery of health care are well aware of the stigma that has been attached to many medical problems in the past which has given rise to discriminatory practices. Those of us who have been involved in the delivery of health care recognize that in many instances medical technology and therapeutic advances have enabled many individuals
80010-44l/2

March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
with medical problems to remain active and productive in our society.
For example, epilepsy has been mentioned by various speakers in this debate. I suggest it may well be used as a prototype for the problem I am discussing. It has been recognized that this group of individuals has been discriminated against for many years. We know that certain myths existed in the past regarding individuals with the problem of epilepsy. Fortunately, I am pleased to report, in many instances these myths are disappearing. In this regard I want to congratulate the minister for removing epilepsy from the inadmissible class.
Having said that, I could very quickly give other examples where we have a different perception of a medical problem today as compared to 20, 30 or 40 years ago. For example, our perception of tuberculosis as compared to 30 years ago is entirely different. It is viewed differently by the community at large.
The same could be said of conditions such as pernicious anemia which can now be treated. The patient is no different from the average man on the street who is presumed to be healthy. Other examples are diabetes, cardiovascular problems, many of our handicapped patients, thyroid problems, and many forms of cancer. The point I wish to make is that certain medical problems which may be considered inadmissible today, as epilepsy was in 1952, may appear archaic in the future with the advancement of medical technology.
It is not inconceivable that a medical officer in the future could deny admission to an immigrant on medical grounds and yet another medical officer could permit another individual with the same medical problem to enter Canada. This does not imply that one or the other medical officer is right or wrong. However, it does point out the difficulties of giving unlimited discretionary powers to a medical officer during an era where there are rapid changes in medical technology, and points out the need for an appeal procedure, advisory group, or some mechanism whereby such problems can be judged on the basis of recent medical data. If this occurs, there will be far less occurrence of the possibility of discrimination with respect to health or social problems.
During the debate of the bill dealing principally with Reader's Digest and Time magazines, the minister will recall I took exception to the Canadian content rule. Although I refrained from the use of the word "censorship", the so-called "Cullen Rule" was unquestionably one of editorial interference. During the debate I stressed a number of scientific journals and periodicals would be affected by the legislation, and emphasized the importance of maintaining an environment in which the free flow of scientific information would be permitted in the international community. That fundamental principle is once again expressed in the immigration objective dealing with the facilitation of visitors in Canada for the purpose of fostering trade and commerce, tourism, cultural and scientific activities, and international understanding.
The minister knows my concern for the free flow of information in the scientific community. Again it is readily apparent the regulations will determine the government's policy with

respect to this fundamental principle, and I hope the minister will take the opportunity to clarify the government's position during the standing committee hearings when this bill is being examined very carefully.
I wish to make a few brief comments regarding the immigration of medical personnel into Canada. Let me emphasize that the comments I make with respect to the medical profession should not be viewed in isolation but are readily identifiable in other disciplines.
The Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada in presenting their brief to the Special Joint Committee of Parliament on Immigration failed to address itself to the commonly held myth that the medical profession is a "closed shop" and determines the number of Canadians students admitted to medical schools.
Historically, Canada has benefited from the immigration of exceptionally talented physicians. They have played an important role in serving the public in varying capacities ranging from family physicians to leaders in the academic and research community. Interrelated with this policy of immigration is the simple economic fact that it has been less costly for the government to import undergraduate students than to train them. Today foreign medical graduates comprise about one half of all the specialists certified by the College, and the majority of these remain in Canada to practice their specialty.
There is, however, another side of the scenario as well as the economic implications. First, there is the moral question arising from the acceptance of a significant number of specialist physicians from developing countries where their professional skills are in demand. A case can be made that Canada has developed to the point at which we should be a net exporter of health services rather than importer of health services.
The second point raised by the College is that an open door policy encourages "reverse discrimination" under which it is possible for foreign medical graduates to enter our system while highly qualified Canadian students are denied entrance into Canadian medical schools because of the large number of applicants with superior scholastic records. The brief states:
Canada should move toward training sufficient undergraduate medical students to meet the needs of the country as a whole. We should look forward to being able to say to Canadian citizens: There are enough Canadian students to satisfy our needs; there are enough graduate programs to satisfy the requirements of these students if they all stay in Canada, and there are enough jobs for them all if they choose to stay here. Some will go to the United States, or to Britain or to other countries in Europe. We shall be able to accommodate some foreign medical graduates of a calibre equal to our own. There will continue to be movement across national borders.
The long term goal for Canada has been adequately outlined in the College's summary. Canada should be self-sufficient in physician manpower, maintaining a balance and ongoing emigration of specialist physicians, and adhering to the historical position that this country welcomes talented new citizens.
As I stated previously, the comments I have made with respect to the medical profession are relevant to other disciplines. Here again the regulations are critical and I do not see
March 14, 1977

any evidence in the bill before us that the government, in formulating its policy, has addressed itself to this important consideration.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on the government's intention, as part of its immigration objectives, to promote co-operation with other levels of government and non-government agencies in determining immigration policy. In this regard I wish to refer to the subject of offshore seasonal help. I can think of no more important issue in terms of co-operation with other governments, and, in particular, with non-government agencies. As the minister knows, it is one which plays a significant role in my part of the country where we have found it essential to utilize offshore help in a number of agricultural operations. As the hon. gentleman knows, I have corresponded with him regarding this matter and I can appreciate the position he takes-that before authorizing the entry of temporary foreign workers the government must be assured that present and future employment opportunities for Canadians are not affected.
It is my impression that the agricultural industry is, and has been, prepared to assist the government in formulating specific plans of action to use the available Canadian labour force. In this regard I believe that Manpower personnel in my area are cognizant of the need to provide permanent, reliable, seasonal workers for the various agricultural sectors. The ones involved principally in my region are farm producers and canneries. What does concern me, however, is that the minister and his officials do not appear to understand fully the practical problems experienced by the agricultural community in attempting to plan ahead for the season in the absence of an offshore seasonal immigration policy.
A major complaint expressed by many farmers concerns the worker turnover. It is not uncommon for individuals to be sent by Canada Manpower, to work for a relatively short period, and then, without notice, move on suddenly to another part of the country at the height of the harvest season. In such circumstances a farmer often has to turn to one of his neighbours for assistance, and it is apparent that any effort to share work crews at such a late date presents problems for the growers involved. I myself am aware of cases where the harvest has not been completed before the first frosts came.
Then again, it has been brought to my attention on numerous occasions that many of the workers sent to farmers have no interest in the crops they are asked to harvest. This is, understandably, reflected in the work they do. Students are an important component of the work force during the summer months but it should be noted that when school starts in September the grower is often left without help. In many instances a large proportion of his crop remains in the fields and he must depend upon inadequate or uncertain help to get it harvested.
Another point which has been emphasized is the advantage of having a complete, homogeneous crew at work in the fields at harvest time. One of the values of the Caribbean work crews is that the experience and expertise they have gained from previous visits is readily apparent on their return to the
Immigration Act
agricultural sector. In this regard it should be noted that any change in the ownership of the operation can result in the sudden disappearance of a homogeneous work crew. I can assure hon. members that a newly established grower not infrequently finds his difficulties of operation compounded as he is confronted with the prospect of no farm labour.
The brief presented by the Landscape Ontario Committee for the offshore workers program outlines very well the problems faced by the industry. I will quote a few paragraphs:
In Ontario, our busy season starts roughly April 1st. It is necessary to use seasonal labour from then until approximately November 15th. Seasonal labour is available from several sources, e.g.
(a)	local unemployed, through CMC
(b)	students, directly and through CMC
(c)	offshore workers
Source (a)-Local unemployed are, as a general rule, very unsatisfactory, for several reasons. In the main, unemployed people registered with CMC, are not agriculturally oriented. They have very seldom had any farm work experience. They are not used to working on the land, not used to the working conditions that prevail in early Spring, in particular. For example: the wet cold weather and the muddy fields. We have had with many other nurserymen, much experience trying to hire Canadian workers for the season. We order these people from time to time. If we interview and hire say 20 workers, after two weeks we are lucky if one is still working. This is one of our greatest problems with local or Canadian workers, that they are hired for the season, but do not stay more than a few days or weeks. After the summer they will, if they have managed to stay that long, automatically become a burden to the U.I.C.
The offshore workers we have are no burden to the Canadian economy. They pay in to the U.I.C. and C.P.P., but do not draw from it.
Source (b) Students: Most Ontario nurseries hire large numbers of students each summer. In general, there would be at least four to five times as many students as offshore workers. For example, one of the average size nurseries employs some 55 people on a regular basis, made up of men and women. They employ some 50 students during the summer and another 8-12 people on a part time basis, as the need requires or more accurately as they are available. They have employed some 14 off shore workers the past three years and find that the arrangement works out very well with the number of regular workers, students, and part time help they have.
Source (c) Offshore Workers: The off shore labour which we have had the past few years is qualified labour. They are fairly well educated, so they learn quickly, they are careful, cheerful, courteous and have high moral standards. They may not be the fastest, but they are steady and dependable, and are at work every day. For these reasons they fit in well to do those jobs which require a certain amount of skill, care and dependability. It has been impossible for us to hire someone in Canada to do these jobs, on a continuing basis (for at least one season). We are certain that agents of the local manpower offices, can attest to this situation.
As I indicated, the key problems as outlined by Landscape Ontario are not dissimilar to the experience of other farm sectors in the community. I want to add one additional caveat to what I have said, a caveat that is frequently overlooked in any discussion of offshore seasonal help. The view is frequently expressed that the program is simply for the benefit of the agricultural community, and what is often overlooked is that the Canadian consumer is directly affected by the activities of the agricultural community. I can assure you that a bumper crop is of little value to Canadians and is of little value to a country in need, a country that is starving, if it cannot be harvested. That is the critical point to be made: the crop must be harvested. In addition, it should not go unnoticed that as Canadians we have demonstrated a genuine concern in assist-

March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
ing developing countries. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in any discussions that I have had with innumerable offshore workers, principally Caribbean workers in my area, the money they have earned in the Canadian context has assisted them greatly in improving their standard of living on their return to their country.
In conclusion, let me reiterate that I have not attempted to discuss the global picture of the immigration policy for Canada. However, by referring to three of the immigration objectives outlined in clause 3 of the bill I have attempted, by way of illustration, to point out the difficulties that members of parliament are having, and indeed Canadians are having, in assessing the immigration policy when the operative portion of the legislation, namely, the regulations and the orders in council, are not available for debate.
During the committee hearings I hope the minister will take the opportunity to answer some of the questions I have raised and the questions that many other members have raised and, more important, that he will supply sufficient detail with respect to the regulations so that all members of parliament can adequately assess, not only the immigration objectives but, more important, the government's immigration policy.
