subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me the opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-24 dealing with immigration and refugees. As several members have already given a general picture of the situation I will limit myself to a few observations dealing mainly with refugees.
In 1969, Canada signed the United Nations convention on the status of refugees. At that time it took on certain legal obligations with respect to the status of refugees. The United Nations convention clearly provided that only people able to prove beyond any doubt their status of refugees are entitled to Canada's protection.
Clause 6(1} of the immigration bill provides that the refugee must meet the same requirements as an immigrant. However, this bill does not determine the special circumstances making him a refugee and somehow placing him in a quite different situation from that of an ordinary immigrant. In several cases, if not all, a refugee may well not meet the criteria normally applicable to an immigrant although his request to remain in this country is often more urgent than an immigrant's.
I think the bill should ensure that officials or those who will have to enforce this bill are able to make a clear distinction between the two types of people calling on the hospitality of this country, our democratic life, our sense of human values, as well as our desire to respect basic human rights to the highest extent possible.
Yes, those who urgently ask this country to receive them because human liberties are not or no longer being respected in their country of origin, and dare stand up in their country against those who want to maintain one line of thought from one party or one principle, should always receive a particular welcome from this country.

Through the years Canada has rejected all forms of extremism. It has looked for an original system based on the integrity of the elements making up our population. Whatever their orgin, the contribution of immigrants to the future of our country can be adverse only to the extent of our own weakness as regards our problems. A strong nation does not need legislation restricting immigration if the immigrant knows that he is accepted because he believes in the values of our country and its contribution to the full achievement of our country's expectations. But if he immigrates to teach political concepts threatening social harmony he will be treated as a subversive element. Canadian people have the most different and the most various origins. Our country became what it is presently owing to immigration.
In this context, Mr. Speaker, let us say that the immigrant coming to Canada wishes to start a new way of living. Our country should then recognize that it is an individual who, in his desire to start a new life, will contribute to the building of our country. We must in fact recognize that if all immigrants coming to our country wish to start a new life with more happiness, when they leave their own country it is often regretfully because of a change of political regime or because of the declared partisanship of their leaders.
The refugee immigrants who face those difficulties show human solidarity as they fight for freedom, for ideas as well as for human beings. They are also dynamic people whom we should consider as good elements for our country, all the more so because a man who is forced to emigrate does not come here to realize a long nurtured plan. For a simple reason of ethics we should consider them with more attention and better help them get established in our country after the difficult moments they lived in their country of origin. Canada should not be a restrictive land for some groups of immigrants, particularly those who come here to find freedom because in their country the right to freedom, to freedom of speech, is not recognized.
This is, Mr. Speaker, the few comments I had to make on Bill C-24 at this time.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill we are debating this evening has come before the House at the wrong time. When we were debating the citizenship bill at second reading over a year ago, I suggested that that bill should have waited until we settled our immigration policy, and having done that it would then have been in order to have brought forward the citizenship bill and debated it. 'However, for its own reasons the government has chosen to present these bills in the opposite order, so the citizenship bill is completed, and we now struggle with what is really the more basic and difficult task of establishing an immigration policy.
We have heard several speakers already in this debate, but I feel that in many ways we have not as yet grasped the nettle of immigration policy.
We have heard some interesting speeches. On Friday last the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee), who is not
March 14, 1977

with us tonight, told us the sad story of discrimination against Orientals who immigrated, or who wished to immigrate, during the period of time from prior to the turn of the century on into this century, and right up until the end of the Second World War. That is a sad story indeed, but one should remember that the reprehensible steps which were taken to bring about that discrimination were taken by Liberal governments under Liberal legislation.
The hon. member did not even mention the most appalling discrimination, the decision to remove Japanese people from the coast and to attempt to return them to Japan, whether they were born in Japan or in Canada. The surprising thing is that the hon. member for Vancouver East sits on the government side, and after his retracing that long and sad history one would wonder what would have brought him to the point where he would have offered to stand for that particular party. It seems to be one more example of the Canadian people being ready to forgive all that happens on the government side, and not just to forgive all but always to forgive all. There have been recent examples of that tendency. The very people whose policies bring us to the point our economic situation is now at, and who bring our national unity situation to the point it is now at, as well as the immigration situation, are the people who are hailed as the only people to save the country.
The immigration policies put forward have a number of very highly idealistic bases. There is much talk of demography and what our demographic policy should be. I think this is a euphemism for a much simpler question: how many people can we afford to bring into the country at any one time? I will admit that there are sad aspects to the question of population, and I will get around to some of those a bit later.
There is a question about enriching and strengthening the cultural and social fabric of Canada, taking into account the federal and bilingual character of Canada. What a contradiction that is! Part of the problem which arises is the problem of national unity which is confronting us very sharply at this time.
I do not know whether the demand to enter Canada has. fallen off at all. I suspect it has not because the situation in the rest of the world gets no better. However, I think people must be pausing now as they consider emigrating to Canada, and asking themselves whether there is some question as to whether the nation itself can exist much longer as one nation. One of the challenges to the country now is that a demand is made on the English-speaking part of the country to develop the same passion for national unity as that which is evidenced in the province of Quebec by those who argue that the country should be broken in two. It is rather difficult, in the face of federal government policy in a variety of areas, for the call of unity to be answered by the variety of peoples who constitute what is in a sense English-speaking Canada. We really must not be sanctimonious about the situation we have in Canada.
If one looks at "The Non-Official Language," the report of a study of Canadian multiculturalism handed down in 1975, there is a page which discusses generational differences in language and knowledge. This discusses mother tongue, and
Immigration Act
the report tells us that fluency decreases rapidly from generation to generation. This book is full of carefully prepared tables, but one table shows that 70.8 per cent of immigrants are fluent in their ethnic tongue. There are various reasons why not all immigrants of the first generation are fluent. Some come as small children, some come removed from their country of origin, but 70.8 per cent are fluent. When we consider the children of these immigrants, the second generation, 10.8 per cent are fluent. Of the third generation only .6 per cent are fluent. In subsequent generations none at all are considered fluent.
We find that in spite of the brave words about this nation being a mosaic of many peoples, about it being multicultural, that those are brave words only. There is a great illusion there. We cannot really hold ourselves up as being that much superior to the United States in the policies they have had, recognizing only one official language.
We have to be a little cautious about the promises we hold out to immigrants now compared to earlier years because they will be confronted with a choice of developing one of two languages, either English or French. I believe they will continue to face the same dilemma of immigration; that by the time the grandchildren are adults, there will be very little left of the original language and not too much of the culture. This is one of the "givens" of the situation, one of the unavoidable facts of immigration. I think we fool ourselves if we pretend otherwise. We fool ourselves even more if we pretend that by some process of federal spending, by some challenge to the people, we can reverse the situation to allow easily the retention of a geat variety of languages from generation to generation in this country.
We fool ourselves too if we pretend there is no bigotry, no prejudice in this country, and if we blind ourselves to the changes that have come about with bewildering speed in the last few years we make a mistake there as well. It seems to me that the patron saint of this country in recent times has not been Valentine but Archie Bunker, and through a variety of things that have been permissible in recent years we have made bigotry almost respectable. It does not surprise me that when a survey is made in metropolitan Toronto the results show a shocking level of bigotry amongst high school students. It does not surprise me to talk to a person about 20 years of age in British Columbia who says proudly, "I am bigoted," and that one then has to spend a long time with that person suggesting that there is nothing desirable about that, nothing that makes it respectable.
One realizes one is working against forces that have tended to educate and re-educate our young people, quite apart from the things done in our schools that have done it negatively. The jokes about immigrants in programs like "All In The Family" have led if anything to a rise in bigotry and prejudice rather than tolerance and understanding. I suspect that some of the people who initiated that sort of programming believed we had reached the stage of sophistication where it could be borne and

March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
the result would be humour and increased tolerance. Everything seems to point in the opposite direction, however.
I suggest we could look at the rise and fall of immigration levels through the theory of the "necessary break". The breaks used to be out of our hands. The first came in World War I when there had been a great wave of immigration; a world war halted that and permitted a breathing space. In clause 3(d) of the bill it is called adaptation. I think assimilation might be a less popular but more accurate word.
The great depression provided another break. During those years there was little hope-and little hope in coming to Canada, so again there was a slackening of immigration. For a period of years World War II made immigration impossible. Since the end of World War II, however, immigration has risen and fallen for some 30 years. This was acceptable in a boom period but it becomes difficult in an economic slowdown. We cannot wish upon ourselves another break that is out of our hands. We cannot bear the thought of World War III doing that. If that happens there will not be any nation left, and if we go into another great depression we will not have a nation either. I suspect we must ask if, as a nation, we should not seriously slow the rate of immigration. I realize that is a question that cannot be asked, and I accept entirely clauses such as 3(f), which reads as follows:
to ensure that any person who seeks admission to Canada on either a permanent or temporary basis is subject to standards of admission that do not discriminate on grounds of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion or sex;
I must accept that. We cannot return to the time spoken of by the hon. member for Vancouver East when discrimination against certain groups was flagrant and blatant. Those days are gone.
One clause we can approve of is that which suggests the government of Canada should co-operate with other levels of government and with non-governmental agencies in easing the road to adaptation of immigrants. This is one of the great flaws in recent years; the federal government has set a policy for immigration and the municipal level has tended to pick up the load, particularly for schools. The load has fallen on the least powerful level of government, that with no sovereignty and no determination of the policy. It has been stuck with the bill and the efforts to make changes and pay for them in education and a variety of other aspects that a high level of immigration has brought about. This is where tension lies, where bigotries become exposed and feed on the fears that come about, particularly as we move into a period of economic decline.
I suspect there will always be adaptation; that we should almost insist upon. It is a great irony that we just passed the human rights bill a short time ago and yet we know that there are a great many cultures in the world that discriminate against women, for example. The very law that we passed is one that if we insist upon it, will run counter to the suggestion that there need be no cultural change or adaptation in this line. We ought to be careful that we do not become wildly inconsistent in our desire to seem to be tolerant and full of brotherhood.
The question of farm labour has already been raised. I think we should clearly understand the bill. If we believe in provisions such as clause 3 that practice will be a difficult one to continue. The thread which runs through all our debate on immigration is this: we must have these people, to do jobs Canadians will not do.
Is it not strange that a country which 100 years ago rejected aristocracy yet retained the monarchy-the notion of aristocracy running against the grain of the hardy, independent settlers of that time-should now seek to establish another kind of aristocracy? Apparently some Canadians are not to do some jobs; they are not to do the dirty, uncomfortable menial jobs. We are to bring in people from outside who, forced by economic pressures in their countries, will do those jobs for us. Is it not contradictory that we should think some jobs are beneath human dignity?
If some jobs are degrading, change them. Do what is necessary to make them fit for human beings to perform. Or, if the problem lies in our educational system and the people we are raising in this country, people who have no sense of loyalty or duty, we should tackle it from that side. But we are on a dangerous path if we think we can have two categories of citizens, one kind above doing any menial job, and another kind we constantly replenish or bring in from outside to do our dirty work. It is to our credit that, under our immigration policies, such numbers in this country are at a low level.
Contrast our situation with that of some nations of Europe who have brought in migrant labourers but have not provided for their social needs. If those labourers had been granted citizenship, those countries would have found it necessary to provide for their social needs. As it is they allow them to stay for one year, or three years, or whatever the period is, rather than accepting them into the community. We have chosen the more honourable route, but if we are not careful we shall depend more and more on bringing such workers into this country. We have already used this approach in agriculture and certain industries. Clearly, we shall need to consider carefully what is implied in sub-paragraph (f) of clause 3.
It seems to me, all the same, that we must have done something right in this country, for we have achieved over the years some levels of common justice, tolerance and decency; otherwise why would we continue to attract inquiries from the countries mentioned earlier? In 1974, 750,000 people inquired about coming to Canada. That suggests that our levels of freedom are not all that bad. We know that the cause partly is that virtually every other part of the world has closed its borders to immigrants and we remain one of the few* open countries. That is part of the reason for the pressure.
The hon. member for Vancouver East suggested that people from Asia had taken a chance on Canada. Mr. Speaker, I can draw on familiar experiences; my grandfather came from Sweden. He did not have much chance in Sweden, and anybody who has seen Troel's film, "The Immigrants", part one, will understand the conditions in which my grandparents lived

March 14, 1977

in Scandinavia. They would know that there was no chance at all for those in Scandinavia.
Sometimes, after my grandfather had been in Canada for a while, he used to grow nostalgic, talk about the old land and say that things were not that bad over there. Whenever he talked this way my grandmother would remind him of exactly what it was like. She had known what it was to labour in the fields without owning the land and without any chance for a shift in social status as the years and generations went by. I suspect that this is still very much the case in many countries, and we, as a country, offer people in all parts of the world hope for a better life, hope for a system of government free and democratic.
May I now refer to a letter I received, in common with other hon. members, when the government brought out its green paper. The document to which I refer is a statement on immigration policy by a group of University of Toronto faculty. It is a distinguished group; there are at least 30 names signed on the back of the letter. There is a dean of theology of St. Michael's College, a professor of religious studies; there are people from the departments of political economy, mathematics, fine arts-the list of names is long. The letter was guaranteed to make a mere member of parliament curl up like a worm on a hot rock. Yes, there was a mass of academic distinction backing that letter. I think all hon. members received a copy of that letter of May, 1975.1 was critical of it.
As you will recall, the green paper was a hesitant document. It skirted around every issue and refrained from spelling anything out. It did not grasp any nettles; even so, this group of academics found a lot in it to attack. If I may quote, they said:
When official Canada speaks of regulating immigration, it seems always to mean preventing too much immigration. Though directly racial conditions on immigration were eliminated from law in 1967, recent practices and pronouncements express the official apprehension-especially toward the non-white or south-European applicant...
We reject the underlying assumption that 'those others out there' are to be dealt with as best profits the entrenched Canadian. The question should not be how many immigrants our existing social system can profitably accommodate, for our social system is changing. The people's concern must rather be to set a social and economic policy, and in that context to set a population policy and an immigration policy. The aim should be to serve human needs-of Canadian (including native Canadians) but also of prospective immigrants.
Freer access to Canada would not solve problems of population or poverty or repression elsewhere; but it would provide one further dimension of freedom; it would offer some hope.
And would the immigrants' gain be at the expense of the present wage-earning group? The government's attitude tends to encourage this notion. It is a notion which gives employers leverage to pit a favoured group of workers against a less favoured. We do not think such a division should be accepted. We doubt that white Canadians have a stake in the maintenance of a pool of lower-paid labour, either within our borders or abroad.
Immigrants do not threaten our culture, they enrich it. Their labour is an asset to our economy, not a burden. A policy of welcome is possible.
I replied, individually, to each of those academics and learned, from the few who replied to me, that many of them had not read the letter they purported to sign. It seems to me that there was room for a reply, that there was no need to cringe and no need for embarrassment. In my reply I commented first on the general woolliness of thought in the letter
Immigration Act
of the academics. I said that one can agree with the opening statement about the "wage of intolerance". That is true.
I question whether the Fathers of Confederation had really considered setting up Canada as a multiculture at that time. They did mention two official languages, but no more. I suspect that if they really wrestled with the problem of mul-ticulturalism they might have spelled that out a little more clearly, but they did not. I think it was a measure of tolerance that they did include two official languages, and we know the problems that have arisen from that decision. My letter continues;
To suggest that concern about immigration policy is a creation of government is simply false. " ... official Canada speaks... the official apprehension." The green paper was long-awaited. It comes finally as a delayed response to public concern, and, as you say, it is tentative. The government was pushed reluctantly into producing a green paper.
Who is the "entrenched Canadian" who can profit from "those others out there"? Those who speak to me about immigration have seen rights promised them in perpetuity stripped away (the British subject, for example).
We have had the culminating effect of this in the past few years with the declaration of the new Citizenship Act. Dismay is still striking hundreds of former British subjects, long time Canadian residents, when they realize they are not Canadian citizens. They are bewildered and dismayed. For anyone to describe those people now as entrenched is making a grave mistake.
They know that newly arrived immigrants have rights the native born do not have. This adds to the confusion because the immigrant can nominate and sponsor, but the Canadian bom cannot. There is no way I can apply to bring a citizen from some other land to this land and have that work. One finds that one has fewer freedoms in the land in which one was born. That is another source of confusion and dismay. I again quote from the letter:
They see Canadian citizenship going at a bargain rate-
That was written before Bill C-20 was passed, with the reduction from five to three years required to qualify. I takes the native born 18 years before he can vote. The immigrant waits three. I would not want to lower the voting age any more. In fact it probably works well at 18. There is, however, still that question there. I then said, and I quote:
Who can be or feel "entrenched" when as you correctly observe, "our social system is changing"?
If in your collective wisdom you know where "The people's concern must rather be"-then proceed to spell out the "social and economic policy", the "population policy", and "an immigration policy" that are imperative. Why that policy should be geared to the "prospective immigrants" I do not see. I know that no country elsewhere in the world is gearing its policies to benefit me should I decide to leave my native land. As the grandson of immigrants from Sweden I stubbornly insist that, should I decide to emigrate anywhere, the onus would properly be on me to make the necessary adjustments.
Your argument for "freer access" is couched in confusing rhetoric. Who can object to "one further dimension of freedom"? But, if the strains of freer immigration fracture this land, who then would benefit?
Finally, you must think again about your rhetorical question, "And would the immigrants' gain be at the expense of the present wage-earning group?" What makes you think that that is just a "notion" encouraged by the "government's attitude"? How can you explain it to the Vancouver wage-earning taxpayer

March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
footing the bill to pay for special classes to teach immigrant children basic English? He sees it in actual dollars and cents on his tax statement. How will you exlain it as a "notion" to the Vernon, B.C., resident whose son is studying medicine in Guadalajara, Mexico-in Spanish!-because he cannot find a place in a Canadian medical school which has a disconcerting percentage of overseas students enrolled?
Confronted by the "wave of intolerance" that you correctly perceive you could do better than to fuel the fire. For the sake of all our immigrants old and new, for the sake of all our minorities, we need an immigration pause to permit the spirit of tolerance to grow again.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate immensely the opportunity to say a few words about the bill before us at the present time, Canada's new immigration bill. It is the first change in our immigration laws since 1952.
My colleagues encouraged me to speak on this matter because I could speak with experience. It is no secret to any of my colleagues that I am a new Canadian, like four million others who live in Canada at the present time.
I speak with reluctance, as well, because as a Canadian who was adopted by the people of this great land as one of their own, having come here as an adult at the age of 19, deep down I still have the feeling that I am in debt to this great land and this society. I have been in Canada for 26 years. I have been a Canadian for 21. I do not think that my debt to this land will ever be paid.
I will tell you in a few words, Mr. Speaker, what my feelings are. I came to Canada at the age of 19 from a country with an overdeveloped culture, and an overdeveloped sense of nationalism. At the time Canada represented a refuge. It represented all those things which caused me to consider leaving my homeland, my friends, mother, father, brother and sister. I felt cheated. It was like when one discovers his father and mother have been lying to him all his life about Santa Claus and the Easter Bunny.
In postwar Germany my whole world had tumbled in. I was old enough to make a commitment at the age of 12 when the war was finished. It was a commitment to something that I thought was great, unique, and worth while fighting for. One grew up a little faster in those days than one does today. My whole world tumbled in after I learned that I had been cheated out of a childhood and a teenage life, which one considers essential.
To me, Canada meant security and comfort. It replaced what I had lost in relation to a family, community and country, because all that was destroyed. I compare myself with people who come to our country today from the Third World. They have learned what it is like to starve. I did that during the last few years of the war. I learned to examine the thin line between humanity and bestiality. I learned that really only a mother has deep human instincts when things get tough. I rediscovered all those great human feelings in Canada.
To a youngster from Central Europe, reading some of the books and news releases, and seeing care parcels arrive, Canada was a land of unlimited possibilities, as was all of

North America, because the American people felt such strong ties to Central Europe-their hearts were bleeding because of what had happened to their relatives and friends. They were very charitable. I learned to appreciate those people, and it became an obsession; I never doubted but that this was the land in which I wanted to settle and bring up my family, a land where everybody is equal before the law and where the only credential, when applying for work, is the will to work and the determination to better oneself. Oh yes, I wanted to better myself and I wanted to work.
My Canadian dream was fulfilled beyond all my expectations. I can hardly imagine what I would have said if anyone had told me in 1951, when I arrived in Halifax on an Italian ship, that some day I would be sitting in this House of Commons taking part in a debate about immigration and about demographic strategy. I would have said; That is too much to expect. But I think I have earned the respect of a significant number of Canadians whom I represent here in the House of Commons, who have asked me to speak for them, and who have given me credit for what I have achieved, not only for myself and my family but for the community in which I live and the area in which I settled. And I did settle in one of the frontier areas, and I have no hang-up about the suggestion that more immigrants should do the same. Perhaps I adopted the right attitude. My wife came here two years after I did.
I wanted to be a Canadian as soon as possible. I felt I had nothing to go back to and I applied for citizenship after five years. Looking back, though, I realize I did not really become a Canadian until seven years later-the first time I could afford to go back to my homeland and visit my father and mother and my family. When I got back to Canada and stepped off the plane in Edmonton I knew, then, that I was a Canadian. I had not known until them. I could really assess the potential this great country holds for those who make a commitment to it. My spirit was set free here and I achieved all my goals, including some I had not even set.
Now, as I look at this bill and the changes in the legislation,
I begin to question whether the kind of freedom, the kind of achievement I was able to accomplish, would be possible for immigrants who come to our shores in the future. I must admit, of course, that today we must take account of the fact that over the last 25 years we have, in a sense, created a unique cultural identity and that we have, of course, the right and the responsibility to enrich and strengthen this cultural and social fabric. But how was this identity achieved, how did it evolve? We cannot overlook the fact that the identity, such as it is today, and the cultural basis, such as it is, have been established or achieved through the efforts of people who came mainly from Europe, people who enjoyed an ecumenical relationship in a religious sense, people who reflect a common denominator. Historically, the Anglo-Saxons came from Germany. It was two founding nations which laid the basis of the culture with which we identify today.
In each of the post-war periods people came here from war torn countries to find a new beginning, and most of them achieved their goals. Most of them became integrated into our
March 14, 1977

society. I can recall the days when four or five hundred people in Toronto would turn out for a social gathering run by the German club. Today one would have to look all over the city to find 40. They have all become integrated into the society we have established-and so they should have.
Today, things are changing. The fact is we have not managed well in an economic sense. In terms of the standard of living, we are not No. 3 any more in the world but No. 10 or No. 11. Our land is not as attractive to Europeans as it once was. We still find Europeans coming here, but they do so mainly to join members of their families who arrived here years ago.
The main flow of immigrants today is from Third World countries. These are people who possess entirely different social values, fundamentally different religions, fundamentally different behavioural attitudes toward society. Our immigration policies must, of course, be structured in an attempt to find a way to integrate these people into the system we have established. There will be discrimination, as there already has been, against these people. I should like to think I was never discriminated against. I know I was not. My commitment was always firm. Since I came here I have spoken English in the home because I wanted my children to be able to speak freely, without accent, while they attended school. I assimilated into the society as quickly as I could. But the people I am speaking about would find it much more difficult to do so. This bill will make it even more difficult for them because it contains some clauses which will be a serious affront to the freedom we enjoy in this country.
You cannot legislate against discrimination no matter how many immigration or human rights bills you bring before the House of Commons, particularly when you deliberately establish immigrant ghettos in areas of our land such as our cities or in the frontier areas. There will be restrictions against those new immigrants for no other reason than that they must work within the framework of our present social and cultural fabric. They will not have the same freedom that I have in making a contribution to the cultural evolution of this land. We have now set ourselves up as the demagogues who direct the further cultural revolution. We are doing this through the CBC and we are doing it by restricting foreign publications from coming into our country. These people will not be allowed to make the kind of contribution that I did.
I want to give an illustration and to cite an example of what I am saying. I can recall the time when I was working in a mine. There were no delicatessen stores there that we have everywhere today, and we were thirsty for a glass of wine with a meal. We wanted very much to go into a restaurant and enjoy a good meal with a glass of wine. It took a while for us to adjust to the fact that one had to spice one's meat in the restaurant with salt and pepper, because one does not do that where I come from in the Black Forest area. The meals there are spiced, and if you do not like the way the food is prepared in one restaurant, you go to another one. That adjustment was
Immigration Act
not too hard, but one had acquired a certain taste before coming to this country, and customs are hard to break.
I recall that there was nowhere I could buy, for instance, European sausage because there was a law in existence that any meat made into sausage had to be cooked. That ruled out all the fancy sausages that the Poles, the Germans, and the Ukrainians make which are made from smoked meat. I had some friends who were also from central Europe. They saved some money and set themselves up as businessmen. They set up a delicatessen store. They moved to Vancouver. They were able, they had determination, and they worked hard to change that particular law. Several of them became millionnaires in the delicatessen business when they started to make this fancy European sausage. A few years later one could enjoy a glass of wine with a meal in some of the better restaurants, and lo and behold in the last few years you are able to read on the label of your wine bottle the year the wine was made and whether the wine is from the Rhine, the Moselle or the great wine growing areas in France. So in a remote sense I have made a contribution to the evolution of our culture because it is now an in thing to go to a good restaurant and to eat a well spiced meal with a glass of wine.
What about these new immigrants who are now being asked to conform to what is here? What contribution will they be able to make? What contribution will they be allowed to add to our society? In my opinion the Immigration Act does not need to spell out that we should foster the development of a strong and viable economy and the prosperity of all regions of Canada. Apart from the great freedom we have enjoyed so far in this country, there is only one reason why immigrants come here, that is to be prosperous, to achieve a degree of prosperity for their families and themselves, and in so doing to contribute to the prosperity of our society as a whole. Indeed our economic welfare will depend on a prudent and imaginative immigration policy. If one considers that one out of six Canadians today was not born here, and that all but half a million of us who are not of native ancestry come from immigrant stock, it is not hard to imagine that a further increase in our industrial capacity and in our gross national product will depend on the number and types of immigrants which our country will attract in the future.
What about the freedom which once attracted people from all parts of the globe? This brings me to the great philosophical expression of what the main purpose of this new policy is. It reads:
It is to support the attainment of such demographic goals as may be established by the government of Canada from time to time in respect of the size, rate of growth, structure and geographic distribution of the Canadian population.
Here is another very serious restriction on the freedom that any future Canadians will enjoy. We will now have to rely on them to develop the frontier areas in the underdeveloped regions of our country. We have to rely on the immigration policy for regional development. I sympathize with the government, of course. Everything else has failed. Our Regional Development Incentives Act has not worked. Canadians want to go where they can achieve for themselves the best standard

March 14, 1977
Immigration Act
of living, and that is in our cities. I look at other more advanced industrial nations and, if I may be allowed to make a comparison, if I look at West Germany, for instance, a country with 66 million people, I find that there are two cities in Canada that have a greater population than any city there.
Any attempt the government has made to decentralize our population, any previous attempt in demographic strategy, has failed. So we are now looking to the Immigration Act to develop our frontier areas. What will that mean? It will mean that if, as we have said, we wish to develop the potential of north eastern British Columbia, in which lies vast resources of energy, particularly coal, we will tell the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), after consultation with the province and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), that we need 12,000 coal miners for that area in British Columbia. He will then send his people all across the world to find 12,000 coal miners.
Of course there is no explanation for the fact that the Hindus and the Pakistanis are most likely to work in the saw mills. They will find work in north eastern British Columbia because there is a heavy demand for saw mill workers there in spite of the high unemployment figures. I suppose that the Italians and the Greeks will work in the mines-I do not know who will work in the coal mines. What we will be doing is establishing ethnic immigrant ghettos in these frontier areas in addition to the ghettos we have already established in our cities. That is a very serious affront to civil liberty, freedom of movement, and the cardinal principles of democracy and freedom which I and all Canadians have enjoyed so far.
There will now be conditions attached to immigration. Immigrants will have to conform to our social structure, and they will have to move into certain areas. But how long will they have to stay there? Will there be a date attached to it? Do they have to stay there two years? The region I come from was not developed by people who were forced to live there. Every day industries grow and corporations move into areas to take over from the small businessmen who developed them in the first place.
Corporate executives are transferred into Prince George, I suppose, as a penalty. They would much rather be in some head office in Toronto. Every minute of their time spent there is a nightmare for them. A person cannot wait until he has enough seniority in his company or within the civil service structure to move to Victoria, Vancouver, Ottawa or Toronto. He does not really contribute anything to that area because he does not even like it there, nor will immigrants who are forced to move to places like the Quintette mountains to develop a coal mine. Those immigrants will hate every minute of it, and they will be very anxious to see the day when they will be allowed to become full-fledged Canadians after perhaps three years, and when they can move out of the hell holes to which they have been sent.
This is a very serious matter, and in my judgment this bill will discriminate against people who will be offered refuge in
(Mr. Oberle.]
our country and who will be told when they come here that they will have almost equal rights except the right to vote in elections because they will not have equal rights. They will not have the kind of freedom previous immigrants have enjoyed.
I am more concerned about what the bill does not say then what it does. I would like to know more about the people who will make the regulations and the people who will consult with other governments and with other interested groups about the demographic strategy and about the placement of immigrants. I would like to know who will make a value judgment about a person's capability in our social structure, or a value judgment as to where in this country these people can make their contributions. Will we continue to have the kind of silliness and stupidity which were inherent in previous regulations when some peole came to our country to get the feel of it, discovered that they liked it, wanted to apply, and had to leave the country before they could apply? But before they left the country they had to hire a lawyer.
I and I am sure many of my colleagues-have several cases on file about people who had to see a lawyer with whom they made a deal to work on their behalf while they were gone.
I can think of one particular case which I am sure the minister remembers. I am thinking of the case of a Chilean family which was located in Prince George. They should have been allowed to stay here. They assimilated well into the Prince George scene. There were letters from service clubs, from individuals, and from the mayor saying that the man had a job. He was a refugee. He could not be sent back to his country, yet the committee, or whoever it was, ruled that he was not a refugee under the regulations established by the minister.
This family had to leave, but they were told not to worry. They were told that all they had to do was get out of the country, apply, and that they would be brought back in somehow. However, they did not trust the system very much, so they hired a lawyer to look after their interests. Three months later they came back. They had to travel all the way to Spain with all their children and come back, and now they are back in Prince George. The father is working at his old job now, and everything is as it should have been in the first place, except for the fact that for the next 25 years they will be paying a lawyer's bill, and they do not even know how much it is. The lawyer probably asked me and some of my colleagues to do all the dirty work, but he is the one who will be sending a bill. There is a price for those people to come to this country, and at this moment they do not even know what it is, but I intend to find out.
Who makes these silly regulations, and how do they fit into the fundamental principle which should be attached to the immigration policy of a country like Canada which espouses democratic principles and fundamental civil rights and liberties? I am disappointed that this bill does not add anything; it takes something away from the things which I thought made this country great.
Of course there are reasons for the bill, and I can understand them, but we have not been very skillful disguising the
March 14, 1977

true intent. The government did not hear what it wanted to hear in the debate which was carried out across the country. The government was told about discrimination and about the need to close our borders to immigrants, so the government had to come up with something. The information did not come from the green paper. The government had to come up with something, and it really does not fit into our scene at all.
The multicultural dream was just a dream, because one of our founding cultures felt threatened by the fact that other cultures should find fulfilment in this society. I for one am not offended by the fact that I should attune to one of the founding cultures which made this country great. I felt that was a condition and a commitment which I had to make when I came here, but why put on this charade? Why say that our identity is one of many cultures? Why do we not spell it out as it is, and why are we not honest with people? Why does it always have to be the devious way? Why does the government always have to work behind people's backs? This bill spells out for the first time the objectives of Canadian immigration policy in philosophical terms, but it falls short of what most of us expected after the charade which was perpetrated by this government.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even with my short experience in the House of Commons I have no hesitation in stating that this is one of the most important pieces of legislation this august body will face in some time. Here we are after many years attempting to determine just what kind of immigration policy the country should have, keeping in mind our goals and what we would like to have in terms of a greater Canada.
I hear a lot about the founding races, and I know what that means, but I want to tell the House that in his wisdom my father, during the first world war, came to this country from St. Vincent, British West Indies, and my mother hailed from Jamaica, of the British West Indies at that time. They had a hell of a time when they came here, but what sticks out in my mind is that of all the countries to which they could have gone they picked this country.
As a result of the beautiful union which occurred when they arrived in this country of mine, I was pleased to be a first generation Canadian. When I listen to people throughout this land who indicate to me that because people such as I have just referrred to, my mother and father, had a different social background, that they could not integrate, could not face the problems of this country, could not make a concrete contribution, then I want to reflect back on my childhood and start punching. That is the way I used to bring about racial harmony.
When I hear this nonsense expressed by certain people who ought to know better, I thank God that my seatmate, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), requested that I seek election to this House of Commons.

speechtext:
At one time a person of my particular hue, being a member of the visible minority-a black man or a black woman-was not accepted by any of the main line parties. Let us acknowledge history. They did not want you; they did not ask you; they thought you could not make a contribution.
I hear a lot about the Anglophone and the Francophone. Every now and again we have to sit back and look at who has done the hard work in this country in order to bring it to the position it is in now-people who took it upon themselves to say that all they wanted was an opportunity to work, and notwithstanding the horrendous attitudes that prevented them from getting ahead, they were prepared to come here in order to grasp opportunities and in order to help the country. That is the kind of stock I come from; that is the message I would continue to preach.
I wanted to be a member of the special joint committee on immigration. In the local newspapers of Ottawa, Vancouver, and all the big cities I read about attitudes that I knew existed. I wanted to find out their extent; I wanted to determine to what extent the country is multiracial and multicultural. Make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, at one time it was not multiracial or multicultural. It was strictly WASP. When I think of the changes over the years from the White Anglo Saxon Protestant attitude to one of multicultural and multiracial acceptance, I know that is what is making this nation great.
Do not let us downplay this multicultural and multiracial aspect. At one time no one would admit that is what this country is all about. But it is what this country is all about. It is a country of the beautiful mosaic; it is a country where the arms of compassion, of friendship, stretch around the entire world.
During the committee hearings, however, I saw the bigots; I saw the racists, black and white. I saw the WASPS. I saw the Western Guard. I saw them all in action.
I want to say that in my 55 years, knowing what went on in the past, seeing what is going on today, I know that the attitudes of these small groups here and there, whose vocal, poisoned, disruptive and dangerous philosophy of superiority is based on race, can only bring about division, hate, suspicion, fear, and violence. It is unfortunate that so much of that small vocal minority gets so much attention, and yet it should get that attention because I know; you know, Mr. Speaker; we all know that we cannot afford such attitudes, and it is my view that Canadians do not want them.
I appreciate the new attitude at the courts, Mr. Speaker. I will not spell that out, but it is said that racial attacks will be dealt with more harshly. Some people may say "I am English and white; should the same type of treatment not be meted out to the person who attacks me because I am English?" That is a foolish and irresponsible argument. When you are part of the visible minority you cannot hide. If you cannot get along because you are Francophone, all you have to do is become Anglophone and move anywhere in the world and you will be accepted if you so desire. If you are Anglophone and want to become Francophone, you can do it by learning the language

March 14, 1977
Adjournment Debate
and moving anywhere in the world. But, Mr. Speaker, when you are a member of the visible minority you cannot do that. You cannot change your name and you cannot hide. You cannot learn another language and hide. You are a member of the visible minority, and as such you stand out.
That is why I appreciate the courts moving in the direction they are today. It is about time. That is why I can appreciate the Ontario Human Rights Commission and the job it is trying to do, even though it may be questioned at times. It may be an impossible job, but it is attempting to bring about a proper attitude. That is why I can appreciate the honourable Roy McMurtry, Attorney General of Ontario. I am not singling him out because he is Conservative but because he seems to be one of the champions of those who feel the poisonous arrows of injustice. He is speaking out on their behalf.
That is why I can appreciate what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) had to say on the introduction of the human rights legislation. Even though we have reservations with respect to that bill, at least we are moving in the direction where people who have long suffered and faced obstacles, and on occasion have surmounted those obstacles, can have hope and faith in government.
That is why I can appreciate the introduction of the antihate literature bill. Some people might say we are infringing on the right to freedom of speech. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, freedom of speech can only go so far with me. When I find that freedom of speech affects a human being to the extent that the person believes himself or herself to be a second class citizen, and so becomes possessed of a feeling of uselessness, then I step in. That can be the end of freedom of speech. You can equate it to yelling fire in a theatre where there are hundreds of people but no fire. Freedom of speech goes just so far. Mr. Speaker, I am just getting started, but it is now ten o'clock.

subtopic: HEALTH-PROPORTION OF CARE COSTS ATTRIBUTABLE TO DISEASES RELATED TO ALCOHOL AND TOBACCO
HEALTH-PROPORTION OF CARE COSTS ATTRIBUTABLE TO DISEASES RELATED TO ALCOHOL AND TOBACCO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as reported on page 1329 of Hansard for November 24 last, I asked the minister a question about rising health care costs. I wanted to know what percentage of those costs could be traced back to cigarette smoking and alcohol. The minister stated that he had actually cut health care expenditures by $42 million.

I am glad to note the presence of the minister this evening. I appreciate some of the things he has done in the health care field, but do not appreciate his cutting health care expenditures by $42 million and all that means. What does it mean, Mr. Speaker? It means that the provinces are to be deprived of millions of dollars. In the long run that surely means that the quality of the health care of the patient, the taxpayer of this country, will be lower. The taxpayer will suffer when we close down hospitals, when we close wings, when we take nurses off floors. Yes, the patient will suffer when we reduce the quality of health care.
The question remains, how real is that expenditure cut of $42 million, because over-all government expenditures are to rise by more than 15 per cent? Here the minister is cutting health care costs; and health care is one of our most important social fields.
I want to know two things, Mr. Speaker. I do not know how much the minister will save; I know that. I want to know what part of those health care costs were attributable to conditions related to cigarette smoking, and what part to the consumption of alcohol? Actually I want to know, in terms of health care costs, just how much cigarette smoking and alcohol consumption cost us.
The minister has been honest with us. Nobody actually knows the figure. A few statistics will show you that cancer of the lung leads in categories of cancer which kill men. The figures for women are slightly lower. This situation has developed over the last 40 years. Forty years ago cancer of the lung in women was rare.
A committee, headed by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle), was set up to look into this question. We found that cigarette smoking was a common denominator not only in cancer but in emphysema, bronchitis, asthma, and allergies. Findings indicate that cancer deaths in Canada run at between
4,000	and 5,000 people per year, and another 10,000 to 12,000 deaths per year are attributable to emphysema, bronchitis, asthma, and allergies.
The minister stated that fewer people are smoking. He is probably right. I want to know how effective the anti-smoking campaign has been. For instance, do people still smoke in public places in hospitals and health centres? The minister may have taken a small step in the right direction. But he is intelligent and knows he can do better in this field.
I have been able to learn that 6,000 people, up to the age of 65-I am putting it in round figures-die from smoking-related diseases; 30,000 cases are treated by physicians in their offices, or in emergency rooms or hospital beds; and smoking-related diseases account for over 800,000 patient days in hospitals. If my figures are right, that involves an expenditure of about $80 million, a staggering figure. Can the minister not do something to cut this figure down?
There are no statistics available in Canada with regard to the alcohol problem, but United States figures show that between $25 billion and $27 billion a year is spent on treatment of alcohol-related diseases. Reducing this to Canadian
March 14, 1977

figures, which are probably fairly accurate, it would come to about $2 billion. The minister knows that in France people drink alcoholic spirits from the time they are little kids because of their water supply. In that country 40 per cent of the hospital beds are occupied by alcoholics or those with alcohol-related problems. Properly studied and researched, why could this not be cut in two, or even eliminated?
Alcoholism and alcohol-related diseases rate next to cancer and cardiovascular disease as a cause of death and illness. Besides the suffering, financial strain, ruined social life, family life gone, and possibly having killed someone while drinking, the alcoholic may wind up on skid row.
Of those who use alcohol, 10 per cent have a problem. Five per cent are alcoholics and cannot handle the problem successfully.
Alcohol is part and parcel of our society. The cocktail route is part of the program. However, for 5 per cent of the people, it is a bumpy road to hell. Invariably the alcoholic ruins his home life.
I have seen a lot of sociability with alcohol, but I have seen the other side of the tracks as well and it is bad. We have treatment for the alcoholic. Alcoholics Anonymous, and medication help. However, if research could come up with the right antidote for alcoholism, and it were harmless in itself, lives would be saved as well as the miseries and the cost. Remember, with all the taxes the government collects, it is not a quarter of the cost in dollars, to say nothing about the human wreckage caused by alcoholism. What we need is more research, more warnings, and maybe a few more taxes to solve this problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-PROPORTION OF CARE COSTS ATTRIBUTABLE TO DISEASES RELATED TO ALCOHOL AND TOBACCO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously the hon. member will not expect me in three minutes to be able to answer all the questions he raised during his speech. I listened with great interest. As usual, the hon. member made a well researched contribution to our discussions.
With regard to the $42 million so called saving the hon. member referred to, as I mentioned in the House on November 24, this is a reduction in our expected expenditures under the shared cost programs. In fact our cost went up by 12 or 13 per cent. I do not have the exact figures now, but I suspect it would be around 15 per cent. What it meant was that, thanks to measures such as seat belt legislation in particular, and other measures, we have been able somehow to reduce the expected rate of growth in health costs.
As far as the figures he mentioned for smoking and drinking are concerned, obviously we are talking in broad figures. It is very, very difficult to arrive at hard figures. He is right that I referred to the figure of $2 billion, including indirect and related economic costs, for alcoholism in Canada. I mentioned that on November 24.
As far as smoking is concerned, we estimate the total in health and economic costs to be around $500 million in Canada. This is no doubt a very, very high cost. Fortunately we live in a society where we respect freedom of choice of
Adjournment Debate
individuals. The health danger can be fought through education and research, as the hon. member mentioned, rather than mere banning which has proven quite useless in the past. The causes are of many natures and kinds. The solutions will have to be multifaceted. What we need is a diverse approach to this very difficult problem.
I thank the hon. member for again bringing this matter to the attention of the House and the country. If we are to make any real progress in this field of smoking and drinking, citizens must be aware of the problem, particularly young citizens. Those growing up at the present time should be made aware of the real situation and the implications of it at a very early age.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-DATE OF DECISION ON PROGRAM FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION IN ATLANTIC REGION
TRANSPORT-DATE OF DECISION ON PROGRAM FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as reported at page 3803 of Hansard on March 9, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) whether a decision had been reached on the implementation and funding for a highway strengthening program in the Atlantic region. He indicated there was a small ray of hope, that they were getting closer to a decision. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will be able to tell me some definite dates and the amount of funding involved.
Tonight I want to try to impress upon the parliamentary secretary, and through him, the minister, the emergency situation which exists as a result of the almost complete deterioration of the trans-Canada highway in the province of Newfoundland, more particularly in western Newfoundland, which to my mind is the most heavily used and most deteriorated in the province. While I refer to that section of the highway as part of the trans-Canada Highway I do so with tongue in cheek, because to call it that is an insult not only to the engineers who designed it but to the people of Newfoundland who voted for Confederation on the strength of the promise that the highway would be one of the advantages they would receive; but instead they were taken, and taken for too long.
While time will not give me the opportunity to go back in history, I want to refer to a recent statement by the president of the CNR when he referred to the decline of rail passenger service. The trains, he said, have been losing business because of improved air services, and because it took nearly twice as long to cross the island by train as it did by automobile; CN sought to reverse the decline in passenger business by replacing trains with buses and the volume of passenger traffic had increased steadily ever since. He went on to say that the road cruiser service has the potential of being self-supporting since rates are set on the same basis as those of the other two bus operations in the Atlantic provinces. But he also went on to say that Canadian National's rail freight operation is now suffering increased erosion of traffic from highway operators and that its share of freight traffic into Newfoundland has dropped from 87 per cent in 1972 to 61 per cent in 1976.

March 14, 1977
Adjournment Debate
To my mind, this is hypocritical because what he is camouflaging is that the reason the railway's share of freight traffic has declined is because of the complete and utter failure of the company to compete and to upgrade its rail freight service. Mr. Bandeen is correct, however, in stating that in order to retain at least part of its share of traffic the CN has sought to take advantage of highway facilities which are available to its competitors. He goes on to say that CN Express intends to make greater use of truck operations in order to provide service equivalent to that of its competitors.
Not only has Canadian National failed to compete by allowing its freight and express services to deteriorate, but it is contributing to the deterioration of the highway because of its failure to take advantage of a monopoly service which it has enjoyed for so many years. In order to avoid straying from the purposes of my representation, if inded it has failed to live up to its responsibility, and looking to the problem as it exists, figures show that truck transport has increased in Newfoundland by some 95 per cent, and will continue growing beyond the ability of government to cope with a situation which could reach emergency proportions.
It is worth mentioning, too, that in spite of an excellent report in Volume C of the voluminous Trans-Newfoundland Corridor Studies we have only reached another stage at which a commission will be appointed to inquire into the transportation situation in Newfoundland. Mr. Speaker, there have been enough words expressed and bandied about with regard to the objective of a comprehensive, intermodal system of transportation in Canada. For some reason or other the government does not want to realize that the basis of any economy is a transportation system to provide infrastructure support for the potential resources of all sectors of the nation. This base is vital in the Atlantic region to allow our eastern region to contribute to the Canadian economy.
The part of our transport system to which I refer is a highway system which up to this point has been accorded only a passing interest. The implementation of a highway strengthening program is vital to that infrastructure support. A year ago today the province of Quebec received $90 million for such a program, and I can only hope that the government will see fit to construct through Quebec a highway to link up central and western Canada with Atlantic Canada for the benefit of all of Canada. I look to the parliamentary secretary to give me the good news, which should have been forthcoming long before now, on a highway strengthening program in the Atlantic region which would benefit the whole of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-DATE OF DECISION ON PROGRAM FOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to thank the hon. member for the comments he made, but I would like to repeat to him the answer given by the minister on March 10 when he said, "We are closer to the day when the decision will be made". I want to assure the hon. member that now we are coming closer to the day when the decision will be made.
This question has been raised many times. I would like to refer the hon. member to the "late show" on February 22 concerning this situation.


And in order to demonstrate that the minister is interested in the problem of transport in the Atlantic area, I would refer the hon. member to the meeting which was held on last August 31 and which embodied the first discussion between the federal minister and the four premiers of the Atlantic provinces. On February 7 last, another meeting was held in Charlottetown for the premier of the Maritime provinces where Mr. James Morgan, minister of transportation and communications represented Premier Moores of Newfoundland. During that meeting, Mr. Lang reiterated the undertaking of the federal government vis-a-vis regional economic expansion. To this purpose, he has insisted upon the fact that a transport system should be used to achieve social and economic objectives at the national and regional levels and to provide an effective service across Canada.
The Maritime premiers and Mr. Morgan have stated that they are satisfied with the importance with which Mr. Lang claimed he considered the development of a transport system as an effective means of reaching the regional economic objectives. Everybody present at this meeting recognized the advisability of improving passenger services in the Atlantic provinces. According to a joint study carried out by the federal and provincial governments, a cheap way to improve passenger services in the area would consist in maintaining and improving only one transcontitionental service.
This study has further indicated the possibility of compensating the loss of passenger railway service in certain communities by improving both air and bus services. Mr. Lang, Mr. Morgan and the Maritime premiers have accepted the idea that the best way to improve passenger services would be through special financial assistance to improve air and bus services in the area. Changes in existing railway passenger services would occur only later on, for the demand is somewhat weak and the cost of subsidies is very high. It was also agreed that the report and findings should be submitted jointly to the Canadian Transport Commission which will hold hearings concerning the railway passenger services in the area.

I would like to assure the hon. member that, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, the announcement will be made, and the date for the announcement of this decision is closer.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-RECOMMENDATION OF DR. HALL ON TRUSTEESHIP OF PENSION FUNDS FOR RAILWAY EMPLOYEES
TRANSPORT-RECOMMENDATION OF DR. HALL ON TRUSTEESHIP OF PENSION FUNDS FOR RAILWAY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I and railroad pensioners all across Canada are hoping that the parliamentary secretary can inform us tonight when the government will be taking a stand on Dr. Noel Hall's report on railway pensions. I hope the parliamentary secretary can at least give us a partial answer tonight, as this problem has been with us for many years, and it is certainly time for some government action.
I asked a question on this matter of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on Friday, January 28, and it is reported at
March 14, 1977

page 2494 of Hansard. It had to do with the fact that the Hall report on railway pensions had finally been published, and since it virtually threw the question of the improvement of railway pensions back to the companies and to the government, I asked the minister if he could tell us what steps the government was taking to try to improve railway pensions. My specific request was that the trusteeship of both CNR and CPR pension plans be placed in the hands of an independent trust company, as recommended by Dr. Hall, and the minister informed me at that time that the report was still under study.
Just last week I received a letter from the Canadian Railways Employees' Pension Association. The letter was in regard to Bill C-228, concerning CNR employees', pensioners' and beneficiaries' trust funds. Bill C-228 is a private member's bill which was presented by the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay). This private member's bill is a cruel hoax which tries to kid pensioners that a private member's bill will increase their pensions. That is a lot of nonsense. The letter states:
Bill C-228 is a private member's bill which received first reading on October 22, 1976. This bill, if enacted, would exempt Canadian National Railway Company from its legal obligation to pay into the CNR Pension Trust Funds the sums of money required annually in order to comply with the Pension Benefits Standards Act.
If Bill C-228 were enacted, many millions of dollars now being paid into the Pension Trust Funds by CNR each year could be deferred. That money would continue to be owed by CNR and an interest rate of 7V4 per cent per annum would be charged to CNR and credited to the pension funds as it became due each year. When the current interest rate for money is approximately 10 per cent, it is to be expected that CNR, if this bill were passed, would not pay any money into the pension trust funds probably for many years, and certainly not until interest rates came down to less than l'h per cent per annum.
We want action from the government in dealing with the Noel Hall report. The government has had the report since January 20, and it is time we heard something, and not by way of a private member's bill.
In addition, the letter goes on:
If CNR had paid their pension obligations from the beginning, as their employees have done, the pension trust funds might now be fully funded. If those funds had been properly invested, inflation and the indexing of pensions would likely not be the insurmountable problem they appear to be today.
Dr. Hall has recommended '... That the trusteeship of both CNR and CPR pension plans be removed from the hands of the Boards of Directors of the respective companies... '.
On behalf of Canadian Railways Employees' Pension Association, we recommend to you that, if and when Bill C-228 is called for second or third reading, you vote against it.
I will certainly be voting against it.
If a bill is introduced in the House to exempt CPR it should likewise be defeated.
We wish to remind you that eleven years ago the Pension Benefits Standards Act was passed by Parliament. It requires a reasonable degree of financial responsibility by all Canadian employers in the handling of pension trust funds. The pension contribution record of CNR does not warrant special consideration for that Company.
The time for financial sanity in the handling of these pension trust funds is long overdue.
A recent letter by Harold N. Campbell, who is the chairman of the Canadian Railways Employees' Pension Association stated the following:
Adjournment Debate
During the last six or seven years The Canadian Railways Employees Pension Association, London Area, have bombarded Federal Members of Parliament, the Management and union leaders with much of the morbid detail with little or no response.
One is certainly long overdue. We need some definite action from the government because hardships are mounting each day for these pensioners.
I should like to point out that only the Progressive Conservative Party had a policy paper on railway pensions in the 1974 election. The paper is being updated but it cannot be finalized until the government makes a decision about the Hall report. As the railway pension critic of this party I shall make a number of recommendations to my caucus. One is the need for a full review of the pension industry in Canada. I understand that the government is going to initiate an actuarial study of indexed pensions. I am also going to suggest the "heritage fund" concept in order to aid existing railway pensioners and survivors, and will recommend a partially indexed pension supported by matching employer-employee contributions. I will recommend placing the trusteeship of the C.N. pension plan in the hands of an independent trust company, and better representation for pensioners in the collective bargaining process.
In our 1974 policy position paper we called for the extension of the 2 per cent formula back to the first day of service. This, of course, would have to be done through the collective bargaining process.
In order to aid existing pensioners and survivors Dr. Hall suggests a "heritage fund" based on a 1 per cent levy of existing pay rolls shared equally by current employees and the companies to provide full adjustment for past increases in the cost of living.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jacques Olivier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: TRANSPORT-RECOMMENDATION OF DR. HALL ON TRUSTEESHIP OF PENSION FUNDS FOR RAILWAY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
As we all know, Mr. Speaker, the matter of railway pensioners is dear to the government and to the majority of hon. members. We all know that this is a very complex issue and within the three minutes alloted to me it would be extremely difficult to give all the details.
The Hall report contains 277 pages and was tabled and published on January 20, 1977 by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro).
The report deals at length with the Canadian railway pension plans. This is a matter both difficult and complex and it is exactly because of its technicalities that it was extremely difficult to have it translated into French, which explains the delay in publishing it. During his thorough inquiry, Dr. Hall considered a number of issues concerning railway pensions. The issue which seemed to him, in the course of this inquiry, as being the most urgent was the problems which face present pension plans in view of the effect of inflation.
Throughout his report, Dr. Hall clearly indicates that he feels he should avoid making recommendations when the parties to collective negotiations can deal with the matters or

March 14, 1977
Adjournment Debate
problems at hand within the scope of negotiating procedures. The matter of improving railway pension plans is one of the fields which Dr. Hall feels should fall to the parties to improve through both consultations and collective negotiations.
To help the parties deal with the very complex matter of knowing how to protect pensions against erosion of inflation, Dr. Hall made a number of evaluations providing various means of indexing the cost of living under railway pension plans. However, the choice of one or the other of those methods was left entirely up to the parties, that is the unions and the employers, who would take into account their general priorities in the field of pensions, and other fields, where possible. In the course of his study, Dr. Hall dealt at length with comparison of the railway pension plans with other plans.
The pension plans of the railway companies do compare favourably with the best, in both the public and private sectors. However, Dr. Hall does make a number of specific recommendations in an effort to have greater similarity between the provisions of the pension plans of the two large railway companies. And the government agrees with the hon. member that that is a desirable objective.
As far as the trust provisions were concerned, it was felt that railway plans were different from others. As a result of those conclusions and the concerns expressed by the unions about present trust provisions, Mr. Hall suggested that from now on the administration of the CN and CP pensions plans be entrusted to an independent trust company rather than to the board of directors of the respective companies. This is evidently a recommendation which will require careful consideration by the parties involved.
The railway companies and unions are considering the recommendations and problems raised by their implementation. Following that study, the parties will meet to review thoroughly the Hall recommendations. Department of Labour officials will be closely following the discussions between the parties in which the Minister of Labour will take part in due time.
